catalogTitle: צריכים להתפלל ביו"כ שלא יתבייש בן דוד ע"י דחיית קץ הגאולה ח"ו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the forty days up to Yom Kippur as an ascent of the 'mountain of Hashem' in time, and calls on Jews, at the 'midday of the world's Erev Shabbos', to daven on this Yom Kippur that Moshiach not again go out in shame.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with 'Who shall ascend the mountain of Hashem': just as there is a holy mountain in place, there is one in time, the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul, whose holy of holies is Yom Kippur. Not everyone reaches it; some need thirty days, others forty, and later generations were shown extensions to Hoshana Rabba and Shemini Atzeres and, through the students of the Ba'al Shem Tov, to Zos Chanukah. He ties these levels to the pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayeilech and Ha'azinu. He then explains that a Yom Kippur on Shabbos brings a greater kapparah, given because this generation needs it, and that the year 5751 is the midday of the world's Erev Shabbos. After a story about Rabbi Hirsh of Rimanov and preparing from midday Friday, he urges bringing back Erev Shabbos and crying out for Moshiach. He closes with the Yismach Moshe's vision of Moshiach going out in shame, and calls on everyone to make the crown for Moshiach through tefillah.

en: The 'mountain of Hashem' exists in time as well as in place: the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, with Yom Kippur as its holy of holies.
Different Jews need different lengths of time for teshuvah: thirty days, forty days, fifty-two days to Shemini Atzeres, or until Zos Chanukah.
A Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbos carries a greater kapparah, and Hashem gave it to this generation because its low state needs it.
The year 5751 begins the midday of the sixth millennium, the 'Erev Shabbos' of the world, a time especially suited for the coming of Moshiach.
The Rav calls for bringing back Erev Shabbos, preparing for Shabbos from midday Friday, so that Heaven too will begin the world's Shabbos.
Jews must daven on Yom Kippur that Moshiach not go out in shame as in earlier years, and through their tefillos make the crown for his head.

Moshiach's shame at the delay of the geulah

title.en: The mountain of Hashem in time

summary.en: The Rav opens with 'Who shall ascend the mountain of Hashem' and explains that the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul are a holy mountain in time, whose holy of holies is Yom Kippur. Only one with clean hands and a pure heart ascends, each according to how he works on himself in these days.

title.en: Thirty, forty, fifty-two days and Zos Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav describes tzaddikim who finish in thirty days by Rosh Hashanah, others who need forty, and the later revelation, brought in the Bnei Yissaschar, that there is time until Hoshana Rabba and Shemini Atzeres. From the students of the Ba'al Shem Tov he brings that there is time even until Zos Chanukah, and counts the days to it.

title.en: The parshiyos of the season and their pesukim

summary.en: From the Gemara in Megillah on reading the curses before Rosh Hashanah, the Rav ties the levels of Jews to the last parshiyos: Vayeilech with thirty pesukim, Nitzavim with forty, Ha'azinu with fifty-two, together 122 like the days to Zos Chanukah. He concludes that the main time of teshuvah is still until Yom Kippur.

title.en: Yom Kippur on Shabbos and the world's Erev Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains, from the Pri Tzaddik, that a Yom Kippur on Shabbos brings a greater kapparah, given because this generation needs it. He then counts that 5751 begins the midday of the sixth millennium, the world's Erev Shabbos, and explains that while no one knows the end, such times are especially suited for Moshiach.

title.en: Rabbi Hirsh of Rimanov and Erev Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav tells how Rabbi Hirsh of Rimanov, as a young attendant of Rabbi Mendel of Rimanov, asked for a shidduch from a home where Shabbos began at midday Friday. He contrasts the low state of Shabbos in earlier America with its repair today, and brings Rabbi Yaakov Kamenetsky's remark that Shabbos was brought back but Erev Shabbos was not.

title.en: The final generation that cries out

summary.en: The Rav describes the world as a covered pot boiling inside, and brings the Midrash that kingdoms provoking each other signal Moshiach's footsteps. From the Tiferes Shlomo he explains that the generation which cries out to Hashem over Eretz Yisroel becomes the last generation, and he calls for honoring Erev Shabbos so that Heaven will bring the world's Shabbos.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe's vision of Moshiach's shame

summary.en: The Rav retells, from the Satmar Rav, how the Yismach Moshe described David Hamelech asking in Heaven for a year of geulah, and Moshiach going out in shame when it is postponed. The Rav adds that the decision may still be open until Yom Kippur, and calls on everyone to help with teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah.

title.en: Making the crown for Moshiach

summary.en: From the pasuk 'You set upon his head a crown of fine gold' and the Midrashim that Jews' tefillos form a crown, the Rav says Jews must make Moshiach's crown now, so that his enemies, not Moshiach, will be ashamed. He urges a serious Yom Kippur and closes with blessings for a year of geulah.

catalogTitle: קטרת ושיר השירים. (טעם שהצדוקים התעקשו להקטיר הקטרת מחוץ לקודש הקדשים)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Tzedukim wanted the ketores prepared outside the Kodesh HaKodashim because they saw Hashem only as a King, while on Yom Kippur Klal Yisroel stands before Him as a kallah before her chosson, the same love expressed in the fragrance of Shir HaShirim.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara and Yerushalmi on the Tzedukim, who held that the Kohen Gadol should prepare the ketores outside and bring it into the Kodesh HaKodashim ready, since one does not prepare things in a king's presence; he asks why the Torah rejected this seemingly correct reasoning. He contrasts Rosh Hashanah, the judgment of the whole world where Hashem sits as King, with Yom Kippur, when Klal Yisroel is alone with Him like a wife with her husband, who is not embarrassed to cook in front of him. The Tzedukim, deniers of the Oral Torah, did not accept that Klal Yisroel is the kallah and the Chachamim the akeres habayis. The ketores, a matter of fragrance, is the avodah of chosson and kallah, as is Shir HaShirim, which opens and closes with fragrance. Smell was not damaged by the sin of the Etz HaDaas and is the sense of Mashiach. He ends with Rosh Hashanah as fear that comes from love.

en: The Tzedukim held that the ketores must be prepared outside and brought into the Kodesh HaKodashim ready, because that is the proper conduct before a king.
Rosh Hashanah is the judgment of the whole world before Hashem as King, while Yom Kippur belongs to Klal Yisroel alone, the day of closeness when the Kohen Gadol enters the Kodesh HaKodashim.
Hashem is the King and Klal Yisroel the queen, but when they are alone they are husband and wife, and a wife is not uncomfortable preparing food in her husband's presence.
The Tzedukim denied the Oral Torah and did not accept that the Chachamim are the akeres habayis who run the house, so for them Hashem was only a King.
The ketores and Shir HaShirim are one matter: the love and closeness of chosson and kallah, which is why Shir HaShirim opens and closes with fragrance.
The sense of smell was not damaged by the sin of the Etz HaDaas; it is the sense of Mashiach, and the ketores is a love that no sin has damaged.
Rosh Hashanah calls for fear that comes from love, like a mother who holds her child tightly on the stairs because she loves him.

the sense of smell and Mashiach
Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur compared

title.en: Why the Tzedukim prepared the ketores outside

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara and the Yerushalmi that the Tzedukim wanted the ketores prepared outside and brought into the Kodesh HaKodashim ready, as one does for a king, and the Gemara's account of the Tzeduki Kohen Gadol who did so and died. He asks why the Torah rejected this seemingly correct reasoning.

title.en: Yom Kippur: the queen at home with the King

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Rosh Hashanah, the judgment of the whole world, with Yom Kippur, which belongs to Klal Yisroel alone. He compares the Chachamim to the akeres habayis who runs the household, and explains that when the King and queen are alone they are husband and wife, so preparing the ketores in His presence is no disrespect; this is the yichud of the Kodesh HaKodashim, where no one else may be present.

title.en: Who speaks to whom: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur

summary.en: On Rosh Hashanah the King sits on His throne and the people speak to Him, as kings are addressed through an intermediary; on Yom Kippur, in the Shemoneh Esrei, Hashem speaks to Klal Yisroel with love, like a husband to his wife. The Tzedukim, deniers of the Oral Torah, saw Hashem only as King, and the Rav adds that with Mashiach this closeness will be all year.

title.en: Ketores, fragrance and the avodah of chosson and kallah

summary.en: The Rav calls the ketores the main avodah of Yom Kippur, an avodah of fragrance belonging to Mashiach, who will judge by smell. The Tzeduki denied that Hashem and Klal Yisroel are chosson and kallah, the theme of Shir HaShirim; the ketores is the most beloved avodah, done inside. He adds that Avraham's tent is written with a heh, as he first pitched Sarah's tent.

title.en: Shir HaShirim, fragrance and the undamaged sense

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shir HaShirim expresses the closeness of Hashem as chosson and Klal Yisroel as kallah, and that its fragrances from beginning to end make it the same matter as the ketores. Smell alone was not damaged by the sin of the Etz HaDaas and is the sense of Mashiach; the Tzeduki who denied this love was punished through his nose.

title.en: Neilah, Rosh Hashanah joy and fear from love

summary.en: Today too, on Yom Kippur all Jews enter the Kodesh HaKodashim, and Neilah locks them in with Hashem. Rosh Hashanah is a time of love and joy, yet in kedushah love and fear go together; the Rav gives the mashal of a mother holding her child and a story of the Kozhnitzer Maggid's joy on Rosh Hashanah, and closes asking that Jews daven for a yeshuah and merit to daven with fear, love and joy.

catalogTitle: סוכות ממש - ענני הכבוד - נכנסים אתנו להבית

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that even according to Rabbi Akiva, who reads the Sukkos of the Midbar as real huts, the protection of the Clouds of Glory went with the Jews, and so the sukkah's protection goes with a Jew into his home for the whole year.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva over 'ki vasukkos hoshavti': Clouds of Glory or real huts. The Shulchan Aruch gives the reason as the Clouds of Glory, and the Bach explains that one must have this reason in mind, which seems to follow Rabbi Eliezer against Rabbi Akiva. Bringing that the Jews sat in real huts when they went to war, the Rav asks what kind of reminder of war a flimsy sukkah is, since soldiers dig into trenches. He answers that the protection of the Clouds of Glory went with them even outside the clouds, so they sat calmly in huts. Both Tanna'im therefore agree about the miracle and differ only in the passuk's meaning. As the protection moved from place to place, it moves from time to time: the sukkah goes along into the house all year, as the Sfas Emes explains Shemini Atzeres. He adds a count of pesukim in Haazinu matching the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul, and closes with a brachah that the sukkah's kedushah enter the home.

en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva agree that the miracle in the Midbar was the Clouds of Glory; they differ only in how to read the word 'sukkos' in the passuk.
A flimsy hut is no defense in war; the Jews could sit in real sukkos at war only because the protection of the Clouds of Glory went out with them.
The seven days in the sukkah, with the hakafos and the shaking of the lulav, create surrounding protections that a Jew takes along for the whole year.
As the protection could move from place to place, it can move from time to time, and so 'all the citizens in Israel shall dwell in sukkos' even in their homes.
On Shemini Atzeres one sits in the sukkah without a brachah because the sukkah is no longer an object of a mitzvah but goes along with the Jew into his house.
The fifty-two pesukim of Haazinu correspond to the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul until Shemini Atzeres, a longer time given to those who need it.

pesukim of Haazinu and the days of Elul

title.en: Clouds of Glory or real huts, and the Bach

summary.en: The Rav brings the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva and the Shulchan Aruch's reason of the Clouds of Glory, which the Bach says one must have in mind, and asks how this fits the rule that halacha follows Rabbi Akiva. He then asks what the miracle of sitting in real huts was, and brings that they sat in them when they went to war.

title.en: A sukkah at war: the clouds went along

summary.en: The Rav asks how a sukkah recalls a war, when the way of soldiers is to dig into trenches, not to sit under thin schach. He answers that the protection of the Clouds of Glory went with the Jews when they left the clouds to fight, so they sat in huts with full confidence, and ties this to the surrounding protections of Sukkos that a Jew takes for the whole year.

title.en: The sukkah goes along all year and into the home

summary.en: The Rav concludes that both Tanna'im agree about the miracle and differ only in the passuk's meaning. He reads 'all the citizens in Israel shall dwell in sukkos' as the sukkah going along all year, brings the Sfas Emes on sitting in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeres without a brachah, and applies it to a new home being entered at this time.

title.en: Pesukim counted against the days of Elul

summary.en: The Rav explains that the pesukim of the parshiyos read in this season correspond to the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, and brings a greater chiddush: for those who need more time it extends to Shemini Atzeres, matching the fifty-two pesukim of Haazinu.

title.en: Moshe's soul in the Torah and today's passuk

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rama MiPano that when Moshe wrote 'vayamos sham Moshe' he put his soul into the Torah. By the count of Haazinu's pesukim he finds today's day in the passuk of Moshe's and Aharon's passing, connects it to the ushpizin, and asks that they help us take along all the days of Sukkos.

title.en: From sukkah to house, and a closing brachah

summary.en: The Rav brings 'and Yaakov traveled to Sukkos and built himself a house', explains that the sukkah has the kedushah of the Beis Hamikdash, and that the greatness of Shemini Atzeres is taking the sukkah into the home. He closes with a brachah that the kedushah and protection of the sukkah enter our homes for the whole year.

catalogTitle: “ויהי בנסוע הארון” - The Benefits of the Travels of Golus

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches that every journey of a Jew in golus has a hidden heavenly purpose, and that the summer months of Tammuz, Av and Elul, like the camp of Dan that gathered what was lost, are a time of bringing back what was lost on the way to the Geulah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a story told in the name of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech of Lizhensk: one of his yoshvim lost his stipend, set out to trade overseas, was stranded on an island, and in mortal thirst held back to make a brachah with great kavanah before and after drinking. The Rebbe told him that his two brachos had lifted two lost souls related to him. From here the Rav explains that wherever a Jew goes, Hashem sends him to raise the scattered sparks of holiness, as the Ba'al Shem Tov explains the passuk in Tehillim. He ties this to the season of travel beginning after Chaf Sivan, to the travels of the Jews in the desert under the four degalim, and to Vayehi binsoa, a small sefer that will one day hold the story of every Jew's travels. The camp of Dan, gatherer of the lost, matches Tammuz, Av and Elul and our own generation before Mashiach. A question-and-answer session on going to Eretz Yisrael follows.

en: Wherever a Jew travels, Hashem has a hidden purpose: a brachah, a mitzvah or a good deed in that place releases sparks of holiness, while the business reason is only the bait.
The Jews were exiled to accomplish outside Eretz Yisrael what they could have accomplished there had they been worthy, and the months of churban from Tammuz are the main time to do it.
The organized travels of the four degalim in the desert correspond to the four sides of the Heavenly Throne, so a traveling Jew is part of one great order, not on his own.
The camp of Dan, which traveled last and returned lost articles, corresponds to Tammuz, Av and Elul, the last three months counting from Tishrei, which are months of returning what was lost.
Our generation, at the end of golus, is the 'Dan' of Jewish history, whose mission is to retrieve lost Jews and lost Torah.
The tiny sefer of Vayehi binsoa is unfinished; when all Jews complete their travels it will be filled in with the story of every Jew's journeys.
Living in Eretz Yisrael depends on Heaven's permission, given according to how far a soul has been released from the decree of golus.

Eretz Yisrael and the decree of exile

title.en: The value of true tzaddik stories

summary.en: The Rav distinguishes reliable stories of tzaddikim, passed down from known tellers, from commercial ones, and explains that true stories kindle a warm bond with Hashem and show how tzaddikim live. He introduces a story told about the Rebbe Reb Elimelech of Lizhensk.

title.en: The yoshev of Lizhensk and the two brachos

summary.en: The Rav tells of a yoshev of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech whose weekly stipend shrank and then stopped, who went overseas to trade, was stranded on an island, and nearly dying of thirst made a brachah before drinking with all his heart. The Rebbe told him his two brachos had raised two lost souls related to him, and took him back.

title.en: Why Hashem sends a person to Chicago

summary.en: The Rav explains that the world is full of scattered sparks of holiness, and every brachah, mitzvah or kind word a Jew does in a place releases them. With the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of the passuk in Tehillim he explains that a business trip to Chicago is only the bait for the mitzvah Hashem wants done there, and that completing this brings the Geulah.

title.en: The traveling season and the purpose of golus

summary.en: The Rav describes the joyous months now ending and the fast of Chaf Sivan for the Chmielnicki massacres, which opens the sorrowful period of Tammuz and Av. Golus has a purpose, and this is exactly when everyone starts traveling; he says a traveler is watched by Hashem, the malachim and the souls above, and must be even more careful than at home, and that the week's events are found in the sedra.

title.en: The travels in the desert and the four degalim

summary.en: The Rav reads the parsha's account of the Jews setting out by the word of Hashem and explains that the eternal Torah is preparing us for our own travels. The four degalim correspond to the four chayos of the Heavenly Throne and the four malachim of the night Shema, and he brings Rabbeinu Bechaye that the name of each degel's central nasi ends with 'el'.

title.en: Vayehi binsoa, the camp of Dan and the last three months

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Vayehi binsoa is a sefer of its own, and the passuk that Dan was the gatherer of all the camps, which Rashi explains as returning lost objects. The twelve shevatim match the twelve months, and Dan, Asher and Naftali match Tammuz, Av and Elul, months of mending the churban caused by the meraglim and of returning what was lost.

title.en: Our generation as the camp of Dan

summary.en: The Rav says that in the history of Klal Yisrael we stand in ikvesa d'meshicha, the period of Dan, as the Chofetz Chaim said. The mission of this generation is to retrieve lost Jews and lost Torah, as the Navi promises that the lost will be gathered, and he describes Mashiach as opening a great lost-and-found.

title.en: The unfinished sefer and the Chag HaAsif

summary.en: The Rav explains that Vayehi binsoa is a tiny sefer because it is still being written, and will grow into a great volume telling every Jew's travels; it is set off by two nuns, which relate to the days of Mashiach. Teshuvah begins in Tammuz, and after Yom Kippur comes Sukkos, the festival of gathering, when even the tribe of Dan, once expelled from the clouds of glory, returns under Hashem's shelter.

title.en: Mending the journey of the meraglim

summary.en: The Rav sums up: every journey has a heavenly main purpose, and business or vacation is the secondary one. The meraglim traveled with evil intent and brought golus; in Tammuz and Av Jews must travel as Hashem's messengers to mend this, and he closes by telling his listeners to prepare their spiritual valises.

title.en: Q&A: a visa from Hashem for Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: Asked whether moving to Eretz Yisrael would speed the process, the Rav answers that it is not so simple: Rabbi Zeira crossed a river on a rope rather than wait, and many great tzaddikim yearned and were not admitted. Jews were exiled for their sins, and each soul can go only as far as it has been released from the decree of golus; Heaven's permission shows up as earthly reasons.

title.en: Q&A: the dynamic neshama of Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav compares those not meant to stay to a transplant the body rejects, and explains that in Eretz Yisrael a person receives a more powerful neshama: a tzaddik's mitzvos rise higher and a rasha's aveiros do more harm. He brings Rashi on the malachim of Eretz Yisrael leaving Yaakov, compares it to the extra neshama of Shabbos, and explains why some great tzaddikim were kept out.

title.en: Q&A: Hashem's timetable and the months

summary.en: In further questions the Rav says Torah and mitzvos must be done wherever one is, and that Hashem's timetable for the Geulah is His business. Asked about a birthday in Tishrei and the camp of Dan, he notes the two ways of counting the year and says such matters are not productive, and explains that Yaakov took Elul and Adar from the months given to Esav.

catalogTitle: שלימות של מצות סוכה - "למחסה ולמסתור מזרם וממטר"' אושפיזין של יעקב

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a sukkah in its perfection draws down the protection of the Clouds of Glory so that rain cannot enter it, and then presents Yaakov Avinu, the night's guest, as the one who grew greater in the impurity of Lavan's house.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that Avraham's hospitality was repaid with the Clouds of Glory and the sukkah, 'a shelter from storm and rain'. He asks why sukkah, unlike most mitzvos, must be comfortable, so that one who suffers is exempt, and answers that mitzvos bound up with physical life, like settling Eretz Yisrael, require pleasure. Tzaddikim who ate in the sukkah in the rain were simply not suffering, surrounded by its holiness. Avraham sitting in the heat suffered only from lacking guests. The Rav then works through Tosafos, who require that a sukkah be able to let rain in, and the Ba'al Shem Tov's sukkah where it did not rain: a perfect sukkah carries the Clouds of Glory, as Rabbi Zeira reads the pasuk. After a niggun he turns to Yaakov, the night's guest: the angels banished after Sodom found their repair by escorting Yaakov, who did not falter at Lavan's, and the Rav urges taking him into the heart.

en: Sukkah, like other mitzvos tied to physical life such as settling Eretz Yisrael or eating with appetite, must be done with comfort, which is why one who suffers is exempt.
Tzaddikim who ate in the sukkah in pouring rain did not dispute the halachah; surrounded by the sukkah's holiness they felt pleasure and were not suffering at all.
Avraham Avinu sitting in the heat was not suffering from the heat, since his comfort came only through Hashem's will; he suffered from lacking guests, so Hashem sent him guests.
A sukkah kept in its perfection carries some of the light of the Clouds of Glory, and then rain does not enter it; this was the Ba'al Shem Tov's sukkah, not a miracle.
The angels expelled for saying 'we are destroying' at Sodom were readmitted to Heaven through escorting Yaakov, who entered the impurity of Lavan's place and grew greater rather than worse.
Hosting Yaakov as ushpiz means taking him into one's heart and learning from him toil in Torah and self-sacrifice for truth.

title.en: Sukkah: shelter from storm and rain

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that Avraham's hospitality to the angels was repaid with the Clouds of Glory and the sukkah, 'a shelter from storm and rain'. He notes that one who suffers is exempt from sukkah, and brings Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi who moved between sun and shade so that Eretz Yisrael would be pleasant, something not found by other mitzvos.

title.en: Mitzvos of physical life need pleasure

summary.en: The Rav explains that only mitzvos bound up with physical life, such as eating with appetite on Erev Pesach or settling Eretz Yisrael, require comfort, and sukkah is one of them. Tzaddikim who ate in the sukkah in the rain were not suffering, since they felt the holiness surrounding them; one who does not feel it should not imitate them.

title.en: Avraham in the heat; the Ba'al Shem Tov's sukkah

summary.en: Avraham, who had the mitzvos of Eretz Yisrael and milah, sat at his tent in the heat of the day, though he should have been as careful about comfort as Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi. The Rav explains that his comfort was only Hashem's will, so he suffered only from lacking guests, and Hashem sent him guests. He then tells of the Ba'al Shem Tov's sukkah where it did not rain, and of Reb Yitzchak of Drohobitch who came to eat there.

title.en: Tosafos: a sukkah must let rain in

summary.en: The Rav brings Tosafos, who prove from rain on Sukkos being a bad sign that a sukkah must be able to let rain in, and explains it according to Rabbi Zeira, who requires sitting in the sukkah's shade. He calls this reading forced, and with a mashal of a fine tablecloth with a bulge shows that under every forced reading of Tosafos lies something hidden. He asks whether the Ba'al Shem Tov's rainless sukkah was then still valid.

title.en: Sukkah, bitachon and the Clouds of Glory

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem made the sukkah so that a Jew sitting in it depends on Him for the rain, which is the bitachon in the sukkah, and asks why the Ba'al Shem Tov would need a miracle. He answers with the Clouds of Glory, which the Shulchan Aruch says one must have in mind: they shielded the Jews in the desert from the climate, and a Jew sitting in the sukkah with joy draws down some of their light according to his level.

title.en: The perfect sukkah keeps out the rain

summary.en: Through the Gemara's dispute, where the Chachamim apply 'a shelter from storm and rain' to the days of Mashiach and Rabbi Zeira applies it to the sukkah too, the Rav explains that a sukkah in perfection shields from rain; we are not worthy of it, but the Ba'al Shem Tov was, without a miracle. Returning to the Midrash, he shows that Avraham's three rewards are one: Avraham himself was not suffering, but he assumed his guests were and told them to rest under the tree.

title.en: Niggun

summary.en: After a short closing wish, the audience sings a niggun.

title.en: Yaakov Avinu, the night's guest

summary.en: The Rav introduces the ushpizin, the seven guests who come into every Jewish sukkah, and says that Yaakov Avinu is that night's guest, whose greatness cannot be described. He brings the pasuk 'Yaakov sent angels' and Rashi that the angels of Eretz Yisrael escorted him to its border and others met him outside it.

title.en: The angels of Sodom and their return

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash, Targum Yonasan and Da'as Zekeinim that the ascending angels of Yaakov's dream were the angels sent to Sodom, expelled from Heaven for saying 'we are destroying', and asks why they were readmitted now. He prepares two introductions: from the Haggadah's 'I and not an angel', that impurity like Egypt's can damage even an angel, which is what happened at Sodom; and that one who escorts another, or helps him do a mitzvah, shares in it.

title.en: Yaakov at Lavan: the angels' repair

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov went to Lavan, the source of impurity, and needed protection; the angels who escorted him fulfilled the mitzvah of escorting and gained a share in him. Unlike the angels, who grew worse in Sodom, Yaakov grew greater at Lavan, and this was their repair. On his return they met him in gratitude, and he sent them to Esav as witnesses that he lived with Lavan and kept the mitzvos.

title.en: Taking Yaakov into the heart

summary.en: The Rav says Yaakov's strength came from fourteen sleepless years of toil in the yeshivah of Shem and Ever. He asks how one honors such a guest, not with cake or fish, and answers that the ushpizin must be taken into the heart: to learn from Yaakov toil in Torah and self-sacrifice for truth, and to contemplate how each guest served Hashem, leaving Sukkos with a lasting treasure.

catalogTitle: צד א: לימוד מארבע מינים שצריכים להיות "פריש" לעבודת ה'.

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches from the four species that a Jew must stay fresh and alive in serving Hashem precisely in Tishrei, when all of nature withers, and connects this to the halachos of the lulav's top leaf and to the Yerushalayim of the sukkah and Shemini Atzeres.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why the Torah repeats that Sukkos falls in the seventh month. In Nissan nature blossoms; in Tishrei it withers. Precisely then the Torah tells a Jew not to grow old and dry with nature but to keep a freshness in avodas Hashem all year. The esrog, which stays on its tree from year to year, comes first, and the other species are invalid when dry, since 'the dead do not praise Hashem'. He then explains the dispute between the Mechaber and the Rema over a split middle leaf of the lulav: is it one leaf among many, or the continuation of the spine? The top of the lulav, like the head of the year, must be alive. He brings Moshe's undimmed freshness and the joy of Sukkos, and after a niggun turns to Yerushalayim: the sukkah is Yerushalayim, and Shemini Atzeres spreads its peace to the whole world.

en: The Torah places Sukkos in Tishrei, when nature withers, to teach that a Jew must not dry out with nature but stay fresh in avodas Hashem.
The esrog lives on its tree from year to year, and the other species are invalid when dry, because the dead cannot praise Hashem.
The freshness of the seven days of Sukkos is meant to be carried through the entire year.
The Mechaber and the Rema differ on whether the lulav's top leaf is one leaf among many or a continuation of its spine.
The top of the lulav, like the head of the year from Rosh Hashanah to Shemini Atzeres, must be alive and fresh.
The sukkah is Yerushalayim, and Shemini Atzeres is a day that is entirely Yerushalayim, whose peace spreads to the whole world.

title.en: Staying fresh when nature withers

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Torah repeats that Sukkos is in the seventh month, and contrasts Nissan's blossoming with Tishrei's withering: the Torah demands that a Jew stay fresh against nature. The esrog, which lives on its tree from year to year, comes first, and the other species must not be dry.

title.en: The split middle leaf: Mechaber and Rema

summary.en: The Rav lays out the dispute over a lulav whose 'twin' leaves are split: the Mechaber, following the Rambam, requires most leaves to be split, while the Rema invalidates it when the middle leaf alone is split. He explains that they differ over whether the top leaf is one leaf among many or the continuation of the spine, which is why 'most of it is like all of it' cannot apply to it.

title.en: The head of the lulav must be alive

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rema that a dried middle leaf invalidates the lulav, since it is the spine, and explains that the head of the lulav corresponds to the head of the year, from Rosh Hashanah through Shemini Atzeres. The four species sing to Hashem, and song must be sung with freshness.

title.en: Moshe's freshness and the joy of Sukkos

summary.en: The Rav links the middle day of Sukkos to the attribute of netzach and to Moshe, whose eye never dimmed, and explains the special joy of Sukkos as freshness and alertness. He returns to the esrog that never dies and prays that Jews serve Hashem with this freshness.

title.en: Stopping to see where one stands

summary.en: The Rav speaks of Simchas Beis Hashoeva and of Yerushalayim, where people go about their day without stopping to think who walked there. He tells of a dwelling from the time of the Second Beis Hamikdash found near where he stayed, and says the sukkah is Yerushalayim: one must stop at its door and think whom one is entering to.

title.en: Shemini Atzeres: asking for the peace of Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shemini Atzeres is a day that is entirely Yerushalayim and shalom, the ushpizin of Shlomo Hamelech, breaking through the walls of the sukkah to the whole world. Citing the Zohar that one may then ask what one wishes, he says the Levites' song at Simchas Beis Hashoeva prepares for it: one must know to ask for the peace of Yerushalayim.

title.en: Closing singing

summary.en: Singing of pesukim and niggunim to the end of the recording.

catalogTitle: צד ב: בטחון' הסוכה הוא מקיף של חיים (ניגונים)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the sukkah, the shade of emunah after the days of judgment, is a living surrounding protection built on bitachon, and that the simcha of Sukkos is the vessel for drawing ruach hakodesh, which is the power to speak true words of Torah and tefillah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with bitachon: one who trusts Hashem has no fear, knowing all that is decreed is for his good. After the days of judgment comes Sukkos, the shade of emunah, where Hashem Himself surrounds His people like the mountains around Yerushalayim, a protection that is never destroyed. Shem, who covered his father with zeal, earned living surrounding garments, while Yefes earned only the burial of Gog. After a niggun, the Rav brings the Gemara that one should pray for one thing only and explains that all of Shemoneh Esrei is one request: to serve Hashem with a settled mind. He then explains, from the Sfas Emes, that simcha is the vessel for drawing ruach hakodesh at the simchas beis hashoevah, why no one slept those seven days, and that this ruach hakodesh is the power to speak true words of Torah and tefillah, from which simcha comes.

en: Sukkos, the shade of emunah after the days of judgment, is sitting under the protection of bitachon, so one can rejoice even while judgment is not yet finished.
Physical protection like the mountains around Yerushalayim can be breached, but the surrounding protection of Hashem around His people in the sukkah is never destroyed.
Shem earned living mekifim, the surrounding mitzvos of tallis and sukkah, while Yefes, who lagged behind, earned only the burial of Gog.
All the requests of Shemoneh Esrei are really one: to have a settled mind so as to be able to serve Hashem.
Simcha is the vessel with which ruach hakodesh is drawn at the simchas beis hashoevah, and one receives it according to one's simcha in those seven days.
The ruach hakodesh of Sukkos is the power of speech: Hashem teaches the newly born Jew after Yom Kippur to speak words of Torah, which culminates in Simchas Torah.
True speech in Torah and tefillah brings simcha, as Shlomo HaMelech says that a man has joy in the answer of his mouth.

title.en: Bitachon and the living mekif of the sukkah

summary.en: The Rav explains that after the days of judgment the sukkah is sitting in the shade of bitachon, where Hashem surrounds His people as the mountains surround Yerushalayim. He brings Rashi on Shem and Yefes covering their father: Shem, who acted with zeal, earned living mekifim, while Yefes earned only the burial of Gog, and he closes by calling for working hard on simcha with a niggun.

title.en: Niggunim

summary.en: A long stretch of singing that the transcript does not capture.

title.en: Praying for one thing only

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Taanis that one should pray for one thing only, with its case of famine and plague, and asks how Shemoneh Esrei then holds so many requests. He answers that they are all one request, to serve Hashem with a settled mind, as Dovid HaMelech says 'one thing I asked'.

title.en: Simcha as the vessel for ruach hakodesh

summary.en: From the Yerushalmi and the Sfas Emes the Rav explains that at the simchas beis hashoevah ruach hakodesh was drawn with the vessel of simcha, the water coming from beneath the Kodesh HaKodashim. He compares it to the breath of life Hashem blew into man, explains why no one slept those seven days by comparing it to Moshe Rabbeinu's forty days, and says the whole year depends on them.

title.en: Ruach hakodesh as the power of true speech

summary.en: The Rav explains that the breath of life is the power of speech, and that after Yom Kippur Hashem teaches the newborn Jew to speak words of Torah, culminating in Simchas Torah. Ruach hakodesh, he says, is not foretelling but speaking true words of Torah and tefillah, each by his level, and from this comes simcha.

catalogTitle: “ויהי בנסוע הארון” - A Yid's true Mission in His Summer Travels

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the seven pazer notes of Behaaloscha point to the scattering of the golus and to the summer travels of Tammuz, and teaches that every Jew, wherever he travels, is a shaliach of Hashem who must not forget his mission.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the seven pazer notes in Behaaloscha and explains the calendar: from Chamisha Asar b'Shvat to Shavuos the days rise in kedushah, and from Behaaloscha they turn downward, with the fast of the twentieth of Sivan, Tammuz and Av, and the reading of Shelach. Pazer means scattering, the golus among the seventy nations, but seven weeks of nechamah answer it, and the golus has its benefits: Jews were not driven out but sent. Every neshamah, which sang with the angels at the Kisei HaKavod, is sent down on an errand, as in the Chofetz Chaim's mashal of the man who traded diamonds for candles. He contrasts Moshe's failed spies with Yehoshua's successful ones, explains that a person's name is his shlichus, and brings the Ba'al Shem Tov: every journey is directed to raise particles of one's own neshamah. Summer travel to camp is such a shlichus; one must not shed tzitzis or fall as the spies fell.

en: The seven pazer notes of Behaaloscha mark the turn of the year from the rising days that end with Shavuos to the descending days of Tammuz and Av.
Pazer means scattering: the Jews are scattered among the seventy nations, which branch out of the seven principal nations, and the seven weeks of nechamah after Tisha b'Av answer the seven pazers.
The Jews were not driven out of Eretz Yisrael but sent out of it; every Jew is a shaliach of Hashem.
A person's name, given with a measure of ruach hakodesh, is his shlichus in this world.
Every journey is directed by Hashem so that a person can raise the sparks of his own neshamah found in that place.
Summer travel coincides with Parshas Shelach and Tammuz so that Jews can repair the failed shlichus of the spies by remembering their own mission.

title.en: Seven pazers and the turn of the year

summary.en: After a Chelm joke about weeks without a pazer note, the Rav points out the seven pazers in Behaaloscha. He traces the rising days from Chamisha Asar b'Shvat to Shavuos and explains that with Behaaloscha the year turns downward, with the fast of the twentieth of Sivan and the hard months of Tammuz and Av.

title.en: Pazer as the scattering of golus

summary.en: The Rav ties the coming reading of Shelach to the spies who caused the golus, and explains that pazer means scattering among the seventy nations that branch out of the seven. Against the seven pazers stand seven weeks of nechamah; the golus brought more Torah and more tzaddikim, and the Jews were sent, not driven, out of Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim's diamonds and candles

summary.en: The Rav describes the neshamah at the Kisei HaKavod directing the song of the angels before Hashem sends it down on an errand. He retells the Chofetz Chaim's mashal of a poor man who went to the dark mountains for diamonds and came home with rotting candles, and applies it to people who forget that they were sent to collect Torah and mitzvos.

title.en: Two sets of shluchim and the shlichus in a name

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Moshe's spies, who failed, with Yehoshua's two shluchim in the haftarah, who succeeded. He explains that a person's name is his shlichus, bringing the Arizal on naming and Rashi on the angel's name in Vayishlach, and that adding a name to a gravely sick person gives him a new shlichus. In Tammuz and Av, the children of the spies must repair their failure and so bring the geulah.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov: every step is a shlichus

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on the passuk that a man's steps are set by Hashem: a merchant who goes to Australia for kangaroo furs is really sent to make a brachah over a certain brook, because sparks of his neshamah are there. He adds the apple, the loaf of bread and a tree near a camp, and describes how camp can bring a boy closer to Hashem through the beauty of creation.

title.en: Summer travel as a shlichus

summary.en: The Rav explains why everyone travels just when Shelach and Tammuz arrive: to repair the shlichus of the spies. He warns against boys in camp shedding their tzitzis, the reminder at the end of Shelach, says the summer is for recharging spiritual batteries, and reads the Nefilim the spies saw as a hint not to fall. He ends with the hidden treasures of these days, Moshiach's roots in them, and a wish for a successful vacation.

catalogTitle: ניסוך המים: מים התחתונים עולים לשורשם - קרוב לה'; וכן אנחנו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that at the water-libation of Sukkos the lower waters, which wept at being separated from Hashem, return to their root, and that the joy of Simchas Beis Hashoevah is Klal Yisrael's hope and longing to return to Hashem as well.

abstract.en: The Rav asks what Simchas Beis Hashoevah is. At the Creation the waters were one, until the firmament divided upper from lower waters; the lower waters wept, wanting to be near the King, and Hashem consoled them with the water-libation on the altar. He adds the Yismach Moshe: when the Temple was destroyed, the rivers of Bavel wept with the Jews. Bereishis is the root of creation; the Gemara finds the altar's shafts hinted in its first word, the Foundation Stone is the root of place, and Tishrei the root of time. Since the libation is halachah given to Moshe at Sinai and Torah is eternal, the waters still rise even now, and the Jews rejoice with them. So too Klal Yisrael, cut off from Hashem, awaits its return. Dancing, like the waves of the sea, expresses the longing to rise toward Hashem, a longing to carry through the whole year.

en: The water-libation of Sukkos is Hashem's consolation to the lower waters, who wept at being separated by the firmament and wanted to be before the King.
Through the libation the waters return to their root, the place of the altar's shafts, which is hinted in the word Bereishis, the root of all creation.
Because the libation is halachah given to Moshe at Sinai and Torah is eternal, the waters still have their ascent on Sukkos even in exile, and the Jews rejoice with them.
Klal Yisrael, cut off from Hashem, draws consolation from the waters' return: Hashem will bring it back as well, to the place from which Jewish souls come.
Dancing at Simchas Beis Hashoevah, like the rising waves of the sea, is the longing to be close to Hashem even when one cannot reach Him, and that longing should be carried through the whole year.

Tishrei as the root of the year

title.en: The weeping of the lower waters

summary.en: The Rav asks what Simchas Beis Hashoevah is and describes the water-libation, unique to Sukkos. He explains that the lower waters wept at being separated from the upper waters and Hashem consoled them with the libation, and brings the Yismach Moshe that the rivers of Bavel wept with the Jews when the libation ceased.

title.en: Bereishis, the shafts and Tishrei

summary.en: The Rav explains that Bereishis is the root of all creation, as the Ramban describes the primal matter. He brings the Gemara that the altar's shafts are hinted in the word Bereishis, calls the Foundation Stone the root of place and Tishrei the root of time, and concludes that through the libation the lower waters return to their root.

title.en: The libation still continues today

summary.en: The Rav notes that today there is no actual libation, yet it was given as halachah to Moshe at Sinai and Torah is eternal. As the korbanos continue in a hidden way, through learning them and through the heavenly offerings described in the Midrash, so the waters still rise on Sukkos and the Jews rejoice with them.

title.en: So too Klal Yisrael will return

summary.en: The Rav applies the waters' consolation to Klal Yisrael, cut off from Hashem's presence in the Beis Hamikdash: just as Hashem returned the waters to their place, He will return the Jews to the place under the altar from which Adam was created. He brings pesukim on returning and describes the cry of the dancing Jew who wants to come back to the King.

title.en: Joyful water, Chassan Bereishis and dancing

summary.en: The Rav reads 'u'shavtem mayim b'sasson' as drawing joyful water. He describes Tishrei as full of mitzvos, ending with Chassan Bereishis and the return to Bereishis, and explains that the Mishnah mentions dancing only at Simchas Beis Hashoevah because a jump expresses the wish to rise toward heaven.

title.en: The waves of the sea

summary.en: The Rav asks why the waves of the sea always rise; the physicist explains the mechanism, but, as a tzaddik said, science cannot say why nature is so. The sefarim say the waves rise because they long to be near the King, and the Rav concludes that the Jews dance like them and should carry this longing through the whole year.

catalogTitle: סוכה' צלא דמהמנותא' שמירה והגנה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the sukkah, the 'shade of emunah', is the higher emunah of bitachon, through which Hashem shelters Klal Yisroel and sends each Jew the sparks and tools of his mission, illustrated at length through the story of Navos's vineyard.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Nissan and Tishrei as the two roots of creation, and the Zohar's pairing of matzah, the food of emunah, with the sukkah, the shade of emunah. Sukkos stands higher because it is bitachon, the fruit of emunah, which brings simcha; it is Yaakov's festival. Klal Yisroel earned the sukkah by following Hashem out of Mitzrayim without provisions, and the sukkah is Hashem sheltering them like a mother bird over her young; in the clouds of glory every need was met. He then brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that a person's food, clothing and possessions hold sparks of his soul, sent to him for his mission. This is developed through Navos, who did not use his gift of song, and Achav, to whom the vineyard truly belonged and who came to teshuvah through it. He closes with world events, fears about the coming year, and the sukkah's protection for all Jews.

en: Pesach's matzah is the 'food of emunah' and Sukkos's sukkah is the 'shade of emunah', and the sukkah is the higher level.
Bitachon is the fruit of emunah; a person who trusts feels secure like a small child with its mother, and so Sukkos, the festival of bitachon, is the time of joy.
Klal Yisroel merited the sukkah by leaving Mitzrayim without provisions, and in the desert Hashem sheltered and provided for them like a mother bird over her young.
Every person's food, clothing, possessions and talents contain sparks of his soul, sent to him from Heaven so that he can fulfill his mission in the world.
Navos was given a voice and a vineyard for a mission of song; when he did not sing, he lost his right to the vineyard and to life.
The sukkah, sat in with simcha, creates protection for all of Klal Yisroel for the whole year.

title.en: Matzah, sukkah and the two roots of emunah

summary.en: The Rav opens with the dispute whether the world was created in Nissan or Tishrei, says both are true, and that the Torah's root, the mitzvah of emunah, must have a point in each month. He brings the Zohar that matzah is the 'food of emunah' and the sukkah the 'shade of emunah', argues the sukkah's level must be higher, and links Pesach to Avraham and Sukkos to Yaakov, who 'made sukkos'.

title.en: Emunah of Pesach, bitachon of Sukkos

summary.en: The Rav asks what distinguishes the emunah of Pesach from that of Sukkos and answers that bitachon, the fruit of emunah, brings a feeling of security and joy, like a small child with its mother. Yaakov, who went to Charan with nothing, embodies bitachon; a person builds a sturdy house against wind and rain, but a Jew in the flimsy sukkah sits content in the shade of the Shechinah.

title.en: How Klal Yisroel merited the sukkah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Jews merited the sukkah by leaving Mitzrayim without provisions. He brings from chassidic seforim that the sukkah is the aspect of 'like an eagle stirs its nest', with Rashi's explanation of the eagle's mercy, and that the sukkah is called the 'higher mother': Hashem cared for them in the desert like a mother for a small child and like a mother bird over chicks and eggs, as Yirmiyahu recalls their trust in following Him into the desert.

title.en: The sukkah's holy names and the clouds of glory

summary.en: The Rav describes a Jew leaving his fortified house for a sukkah of two walls and a tefach, sitting with bitachon and joy; the sukkah is a 'tower of strength' of holy names that protect for the whole year. He brings a gematria linking the mother bird to the sukkah, describes how the clouds of glory met every need, and answers the question of the Chida and Bnei Yissaschar why we commemorate the clouds and not the well: everything was contained in the clouds, so the sukkah is also a segulah for parnassah.

title.en: Sparks of the soul in food and possessions

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on 'hungry and thirsty, their soul is wrapped in them': sparks of each soul fell and are scattered in food, clothing, vessels and possessions, and Hashem sends each person exactly his own. Eating with washing and a proper bracha elevates the spark, while eating without a bracha drags it down; borrowing, buying and selling, and even a broken glass are explained this way, as is 'the daughter of so-and-so to so-and-so'. Every Jew comes down with a mission, and his parnassah, tools and friends are part of it.

title.en: The passage of Navos's vineyard

summary.en: The Rav reads through the passage in Melachim of Navos the Yizre'elite, whose vineyard bordered Achav's palace: Achav offers a better vineyard or money, Navos refuses to give up his ancestral inheritance, and Achav comes home sullen. He asks why the passuk keeps calling him 'Navos the Yizre'elite' when he was Achav's neighbor, illustrating with a Munkatcher neighbor in Brooklyn whom one would not call by his town.

title.en: Navos's voice, the vineyard and the world of song

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yalkut on 'honor Hashem with your wealth', read as 'with your throat': Navos had a sweet voice and used to sing in Yerushalayim, stopped, and was therefore killed. He asks why that should merit death, and answers that every talent is a sign of a person's mission; a vineyard, wine and song belong together, so Navos was given the vineyard for his song, and when he did not sing he had no purpose in the world and lost it. He describes the heavenly chamber of song headed by Dovid HaMelech, the seven 'voices' completed on Shabbos, and music and rhymes at a wedding as a joining of things that belong together.

title.en: Achav's claim to the vineyard

summary.en: The Rav says Navos was a great soul tied to Dovid HaMelech and Moshiach, and that Achav too was a great soul, citing the Chiddushei HaRim. The vineyard also held Achav's sparks, which is why he desired it, as the Satmar Rav wrote that Heaven shows a person where his heart is drawn. From the Gemara in Sanhedrin he shows the vineyard would have come to Achav lawfully either way; his sin, per the Zera Kodesh, was taking it by killing Navos through false witnesses instead of waiting, and yet the vineyard did him a great favor by bringing him to teshuvah.

title.en: Teshuvah, song and Izevel's claim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Kedushas Levi that the gates of teshuvah stand next to the gates of song, and Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer that Achav did great teshuvah after Eliyahu's rebuke, with the Chovos HaLevavos that a sin can become a person's success; through the vineyard Achav came to teshuvah. Izevel too was from the root of song: the Midrash says her skull, hands and feet were buried because she danced before chassanim and kallos. Hence her claim that the vineyard belonged to those who rejoice chassan and kallah, not to Navos, who did not sing; the rule is that each person receives the sparks of his own root, and one with bitachon receives them easily.

title.en: Yehoyachin's daily bread and the festival of bitachon

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the end of Yirmiyahu, where Yehoyachin's daily portion comes 'from the king of Bavel', with the end of Melachim, which says only 'from the king': Yehoyachin, a tzaddik, knew his food came from Hashem, and the difference is hidden versus revealed Divine providence. He then says Sukkos is the festival of bitachon, teaching that Hashem provides every need and talent for a person's mission, brings the Rokeach on the 'real sukkos' of the desert, and calls the sukkah a reflection of the desert's trust, bringing protection for the whole year.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim and the Mississippi flood

summary.en: The Rav retells a story heard from Rav Avraham Kalmanowitz: when the Mississippi flooded in America, the Chofetz Chaim gathered the people for a drasha and cried out that Hashem 'makes winds His messengers'. The Rav applies this to recent events: a flood in America, earthquakes in Turkey and Taiwan, and a solar eclipse that frightened the Arabs in Eretz Yisroel, explaining an earthquake through 'He looks at the earth and it trembles'.

title.en: Fear of the coming year and a flood of Torah

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the widespread fear of the coming year, including the gentiles' tradition about the year two thousand, and says our seforim also speak of it, citing the Pe'as HaShulchan from the Gra and recalling earlier years of reckoning. He brings the Pri Tzaddik that the generation of the flood should have received the Torah and refused, so it became a flood, and says Jews who learn and accept the Torah can turn the threat into blessing; sitting in the sukkah with simcha protects all of Klal Yisroel.

title.en: The sukkah's shelter over all Klal Yisroel

summary.en: The Rav says one Jew's sitting in the sukkah protects even Jews who do not know what a sukkah is, since all Jewish souls are bound together, and that Shemini Atzeres and Simchas Torah, days of accepting Hashem's kingship with love, continue this protection. He brings the Midrash that the nations feared a flood at Matan Torah and were told it was a 'flood' of Torah, with the Sfas Emes on Shemini Atzeres, urges using these precious days with kedushah, tefillah, Torah and simcha, and closes with a brachah for a year of joy and redemption.

catalogTitle: The Scattering of the Yidden in Golus to Gather the Sparks of Kedushah

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the seven 'pazer' notes of Parshas Beha'aloscha point to the scattering of the Yidden in golus, which Hashem directs so that every Jew, wherever he travels, can gather the sparks of kedushah that belong to his soul.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Chelm joke about the missing 'pazer' note and notes that Beha'aloscha has seven of them. After the climb from Pesach to Shavuos, the calendar now descends toward Tammuz and Av, rooted in the meraglim, whose sin brought the scattering of Klal Yisrael among the nations. On a deeper level, sparks of kedushah are scattered throughout the world, and Jews are sent everywhere to free them through mitzvos and brachos. Everyone has his own portion of creation, and Hashem leads each step, as the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the glass of water in Chicago shows. 'Al pi Hashem yachanu' speaks of every Jew's travels. The meraglim failed their shlichus; the summer travel season comes to repair it. Tammuz and Av, the months of the failed nesi'im, hold the roots of geulah. The Rav ends by telling the bochurim that vacation is a shlichus to be kept with care.

en: The seven 'pazer' notes in Beha'aloscha allude to the scattering of the Yidden among the nations, the reverse of the gathering of the seven weeks of Sefirah.
Sparks of kedushah are scattered throughout the world, and Jews are sent everywhere to release them through Torah and mitzvos; this is the deep reason for golus.
Every person has his own portion of creation bound to his soul, and Hashem's individual providence brings him into contact with it so he can elevate it.
The verse 'al pi Hashem yachanu' is not only history: every Jew's travels and stops are directed by Hashem for a purpose.
The meraglim failed because they went as messengers of the people with ulterior motives; the summer travel season, falling in the same period, is meant to repair their failed shlichus.
Tammuz and Av, though months of churban on the surface, hold the roots of geulah and are destined to become the most joyful days of the year.

title.en: Chelm's missing pazer and the climb to Shavuos

summary.en: The Rav tells the Chelm joke of an emergency meeting because five weeks passed without a 'pazer' note in the Torah reading, and tells the bochurim that this week's sedra has seven. He then describes the period from Pesach through Shavuos as a joyful uphill journey, now passed.

title.en: Down the hill toward Tammuz and Av

summary.en: The Rav calls Chof Sivan a turning point toward the sorrowful months of Tammuz and Av, whose origin is the meraglim. Because of them the Yidden were scattered among the seventy nations, and the seven pazers stand in contrast to the seven weeks of Sefirah that gathered them.

title.en: Scattered sparks and why Jews are everywhere

summary.en: Drawing on the Chassidishe seforim, the Rav explains that fragments of kedushah were scattered all over the world and held captive by the sitra achra, and that Jews are sent everywhere to free them through mitzvos and learning. The sparks are in the food, clothing, homes and streets one uses, and each person has his own portion.

title.en: Each person's portion of creation

summary.en: The Rav shows from the Mabul that a person's sins affect his part of creation, while Noach's portion was saved. Children, a wife, an apple one eats with a brachah and the wool of one's suit are all part of a person's portion, brought to him by hashgachah pratis, as the passuk 'Me'Hashem mitzadei gever konanu' says.

title.en: The glass of water in Chicago

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that a businessman travels to Chicago for a meeting, but Hashem sends him there to make a brachah on a certain glass of water. Even a gentile miner's steel reaches the Jew whose spoon it becomes, every falling leaf is under hashgachah, and walking to yeshiva elevates the pavement.

title.en: 'Al pi Hashem yachanu': every Jew's travels

summary.en: The Rav explains that the travels in Beha'aloscha are not history but the Torah's eternal word: every Jew's journeys are directed by Hashem to gather the scattered sparks. Communities stay in a land for hundreds of years until their task is done and then move on, as with the expulsion from Spain.

title.en: Without golus, who would gather the sparks?

summary.en: The Rav asks: had the meraglim brought a good report there would have been no golus, so who would have gathered the sparks among the seventy nations? He brings the Chasam Sofer's answer from the tefillah 'gather us from the nations': the nations would have brought the sparks to Eretz Yisrael. He connects the meraglim's forty days to Parshas Shelach and Tammuz.

title.en: A person's name is his shlichus

summary.en: From the angel's answer to Yaakov in Vayishlach, the Rav explains that a name reflects one's mission, which is why a sick person whose mission is complete is given a new name. Every Jew is a shaliach of Hashem, placed exactly where he must be, and must return to report that he fulfilled it.

title.en: Failed and successful shluchim

summary.en: The Rav asks whether Moshe or the people sent the meraglim, and answers that they went as the people's messengers with ulterior motives and so failed. The summer travel season falls in the same weeks to repair this; Yehoshua and Kalev, and the spies sent to Yericho, are the successful shluchim, and the Rav tells the bochurim to choose which kind to be, even when picking berries on vacation.

title.en: Tammuz and Av: the months of Reuven and Shimon

summary.en: The Rav explains that each month corresponds to a shevet, and asks why Yehuda and Yissachar lead instead of Reuven and Shimon. Two of the twelve nesi'im failed, those of Reuven and Shimon, and their months are Tammuz and Av, the fourth and fifth, which fell just after the brightest days of summer.

title.en: The roots of geulah in Tammuz and Av

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Satan concentrated on the meraglim because their success would have prevented golus. Yet these months are the origins of geulah: the pesukim of Rus are linked to Shiva Asar B'Tammuz and the Medrash in Eichah says Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av, and the navi Zechariah says the fasts will become days of joy.

title.en: Vacation as a delicate shlichus

summary.en: The Rav tells the bochurim that on vacation they must not throw off ol malchus shamayim, as some do on the ball field, and describes the chestnut tree waiting thousands of years for a bochur to learn Gemara under it. He urges care in learning, davening and every mitzvah, allows exercise for a healthy body but not at the expense of learning and davening, and closes with the pazer's message: be a successful shaliach and turn Tammuz and Av into days of joy.

catalogTitle: הסוכה - הוא עיר מקלט' דרוש על ערי מקלט' ס"ם' משה' משיח

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the sukkah is an ir miklat, a city of refuge tied to Moshe and Moshiach, and that in a time of fear a Jew runs to Betzer, the sukkah and the Torah, not to Batzrah, where Samael and the nations seek their safety.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Yehi Ratzon before entering the sukkah, which speaks of going into exile, and with the Zohar that after Yom Kippur Yaakov flees from Esav into the sukkah, a city of refuge. He brings the Gemara in Makkos that Samael will flee to Batzrah, mistaking it for Betzer, and asks how so great a scholar could err. Through the Rambam's three Torah sources for Moshiach he shows that arei miklat is the one mitzvah never fulfilled in full, so Moshiach, the king, completes the Torah through it; Moshe began it and Moshiach will finish it. Betzer therefore smells of Moshiach, and Samael cannot bear it. He explains that kingship comes from Moav, and that David is its holy spark. Turning to the fears of that year, he says the nations run to Batzrah, to weapons, while a Jew runs to the sukkah, the Torah and bitachon.

en: The Rav explains that the sukkah is a city of refuge: Yaakov fled from Esav to Sukkos, and 'ונס' hints at 'ויעקב נסע סכתה'.
According to the Rav, arei miklat is the one mitzvah of the Torah never yet fulfilled in full, and Moshiach will complete the keeping of the Torah through it.
He teaches that each soul has its own mitzvah, and Moshiach's mitzvah is arei miklat; Moshe Rabbeinu began it and Moshiach will finish it.
The Rav explains that Samael flees to Batzrah because Betzer, the city of Moshe and of Moshiach's mitzvah, is unbearable to him.
He says that in a time of fear the nations run to Batzrah, to money and weapons, while a Jew runs to Betzer: the sukkah, the Torah and tefillah.
The Rav explains that the sukkah is emunah and bitachon, and that whoever has bitachon need fear nothing.

candidateTopics: sukkah as a city of refuge

title.en: The sukkah as a sweet exile and a refuge

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Yehi Ratzon before entering the sukkah, which likens it to going into exile, and calls it a sweet exile under the wings of the Shechinah. He brings the Zohar that after Yom Kippur Esav is angry again and Yaakov flees into the sukkah, and a hint that 'ונס' stands for 'ויעקב נסע סכתה'.

title.en: Samael's mistake: fleeing to Batzrah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Makkos that Samael will make three mistakes, the first being that he flees to Batzrah as if it were a city of refuge, when Betzer is the city of refuge. He asks how a scholar who can twist great talmidei chachamim could make a mistake every child learning Chumash would avoid.

title.en: The Rambam's three Torah sources for Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav goes through the end of the Rambam's Hilchos Melachim: the Torah speaks of the redemption in Parshas Nitzavim, in Bilam's prophecy, and in the three added cities of refuge, which have never yet been fulfilled. He then lists the Rambam's signs of one who is presumed to be Moshiach and of certain Moshiach.

title.en: Arei miklat: the mitzvah Moshiach completes

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Torah needs three places for Moshiach and answers that each holds one of the Rambam's signs. Every mitzvah has been kept, even those never possible in practice, by learning them; only the added cities of refuge are still missing, so Moshiach, who completes the keeping of the Torah through them, is called chasan Torah.

title.en: The mitzvah of a king and every soul's own mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav asks why Shmuel was angry when the people asked for a king if the Torah commands it, and answers from the Tzemach Tzedek that a true king, like David and Moshiach, is batel to Hashem and brings all Jews to that bitul. He then says that each of the souls has a particular mitzvah of its own, for which a person must be moser nefesh.

title.en: Moshiach's own mitzvah, begun by Moshe

summary.en: The Rav asks what Moshiach's own mitzvah is and answers that it is arei miklat, which belongs to the king, the heart to which all run. He gives a gematria linking 'ויספת לך עוד שלש' to the mitzvah of appointing a king, and brings that Moshiach is the soul of Moshe, so Moshe began the cities of refuge and Moshiach will finish them.

title.en: Why Samael cannot bear Betzer

summary.en: Returning to Samael, the Rav brings Tosafos on why the shofar confuses the Satan: what reminds a person of what he fears frightens him. So too Betzer, Moshe's city and the place of Moshiach's mitzvah, smells of Moshiach, and Samael must flee it to Batzrah, consoling himself that by grammar it is the same word in the feminine, which in the sitra achra is the stronger.

title.en: Kingship from Moav and David's holy spark

summary.en: The Rav explains that kingship of flesh and blood is not a Jewish thing, so it had to be brought from Moav through Rus, and that Moav 'exports' kingship, as Batzrah gave a king to Edom. Moav is gematria 49, malchus shebemalchus; David is the holy spark of that kingship, and 'ומחץ פאתי מואב' describes his breaking its klipah.

title.en: Today's fears: the nations run to Batzrah

summary.en: The Rav describes the fear gripping the world over a Yishmaeli ruler in Bavel and brings the Imrei Emes: when kingdoms provoke each other, a Jew should not get involved but hope for Moshiach through learning, davening and tzedakah. The nations run to Batzrah, to money and weapons; a Jew runs to Betzer, the sukkah, the 'tower of strength', as a tzaddik once told people to sit where the sukkah stood during a plague.

title.en: Yishmael: Hashem hears the prayers

summary.en: The Rav brings the Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer that Yishmael is so named because Hashem will hear the prayers of Jews when Yishmael oppresses them, even though his exile is the hardest, as the Rambam writes in Igeres Teiman. A prayer is accepted when it reaches the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, and he connects these to the thirteen rules of Rabbi Yishmael, to the Rosh Hashanah reading about Yishmael, and to Torah and chesed as protection from the birth pangs of Moshiach.

title.en: The sukkah: protection, emunah and bitachon

summary.en: The Rav explains that the sukkah is a city of refuge that gives protection for the whole year, taken home on Shemini Atzeres, and that it is the shade of emunah and the bitachon of Yaakov. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that before a decree bitachon is taken away, and shows from the year's number, 5763, that it is a year that needs the sukkah's shade.

title.en: Yovel, the sukkah, and the year 5763

summary.en: The Rav explains that the sukkah is Imma Ila'ah, Binah, which is the yovel, mentioned twenty-one times in the Torah; the last mention points to the coming of Moshiach and equals 5763 in gematria. He prays that the merit of the sukkah protect from destruction, brings Targum Yonasan on 'ידבר עמים תחתינו', and shows a gematria tying the sukkah's shade to protection from Yishmael, the archer.

title.en: The sukkah as Eretz Yisrael; the Torah as refuge

summary.en: The Rav asks how the final seal can come on Hoshana Rabbah after Yom Kippur, and answers that the sukkah has the quality of Eretz Yisrael, where a fugitive's case is reopened for its merit. He then brings the Gemara in Makkos that the Torah is a city of refuge, and says one's mind must stay set on returning to it even when going to work, just as one still lives in the sukkah when stepping out.

title.en: Running to Betzer, and closing blessings

summary.en: The Rav says the people of Skver have a Betzer among them, and that sitting in the sukkah and learning Torah should be done on behalf of all Klal Yisrael. He brings the Ba'al HaTurim that the fall of Yishmael is a sign of Moshiach, and the Mishnah in Keilim on the sea creature that flees to land: where one runs shows where one's root is, and a Jew runs to Hashem, the sukkah and the Torah. He closes with blessings.

catalogTitle: כפי שיושבים בסוכה כך ממשיכים בחינת ענני הכבוד

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the sukkah is a remembrance of the Clouds of Glory, and that a Jew draws down their protection according to the emunah and bitachon with which he sits in the sukkah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the halacha that sechach must let rain in, and with the Gemara where Rabbi Zeira learns the height of the sukkah from the passuk that the sukkah is for shade, while Tosafos asks that the same passuk speaks of shelter from rain. The Mishnah Berurah gives the intent of the mitzvah: a remembrance of the Clouds of Glory, which the Bnei Yissaschar explains were a gift of comfort beyond necessity. How can a sukkah that lets rain in recall them? The Rav brings the tradition that it did not rain in the Ba'al Shem Tov's sukkah, and explains that the sechach was kosher; it was the Ba'al Shem Tov who kept the rain out. The sukkah is the shade of emunah, rooted in Yaakov Avinu, the source of bitachon, and its joy is the calm of one who relies on Hashem. Full protection belongs to the days of Mashiach; today each Jew merits a glimmer of it according to his bitachon, which every mitzvah needs.

en: The intent of the mitzvah of sukkah is to remember the Clouds of Glory that shielded the Jews in the desert from sun, wind, rain and every discomfort.
The halacha requires sechach that lets rain in; when rain did not fall in a tzaddik's sukkah, it was the tzaddik, not the sechach, that kept it out, so the sukkah remained kosher.
The protection of the sukkah, a remembrance of the Clouds of Glory, accompanies a Jew through the whole year.
The sukkah is the shade of emunah and the source of bitachon, rooted in Yaakov Avinu, and its simcha is the calm of one who relies on Hashem.
According to how a Jew sits in the sukkah, aware that he is under the shade of the Shechinah, he merits a glimmer of the Clouds of Glory; in full this belongs to the days of Mashiach.
No mitzvah can be fulfilled in completeness without bitachon, and Sukkos is the wellspring of bitachon.

title.en: Sechach that lets rain in, and the Clouds of Glory

summary.en: The Rav opens with the halacha that sechach must be sparse enough for rain to enter, and with the Gemara where Rabbi Zeira learns the sukkah's height from the passuk that it is for shade, on which Tosafos asks from the end of the passuk about shelter from rain. He then brings the Mishnah Berurah that the sukkah is a remembrance of the Clouds of Glory.

title.en: A remembrance of comfort; the Ba'al Shem Tov's sukkah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the Torah commands a remembrance of the Clouds of Glory and not of the mann, because the clouds were a gift of comfort beyond necessity. He asks how a sukkah that lets rain in can recall them, brings the tradition that it did not rain in the Ba'al Shem Tov's sukkah, and explains why that sukkah was still kosher.

title.en: Protection for the whole year; Yaakov and bitachon

summary.en: The Rav explains that through the mitzvah of sukkah Jews draw protection for the whole year, as reflected in the prayer to spread over us the sukkah of peace, and tells of a plague when people were told to stand where their sukkah had stood. He calls the sukkah the shade of emunah and connects it to Yaakov Avinu, the root of bitachon, who went to Sukkos after fleeing Esav.

title.en: Simcha as reliance; the clouds now and in Mashiach's days

summary.en: The Rav explains zman simchaseinu: simcha is the calm of one who relies on Hashem, and its opposite is the loneliness of having no one to lean on. As a Jew sits in the sukkah aware of the Shechinah above him, he merits a glimmer of the Clouds of Glory; the full protection belongs to the days of Mashiach, while today, as the Rambam shows about open miracles, we are not on that level.

title.en: No mitzvah without bitachon; the days ahead

summary.en: The Rav says no mitzvah can be fulfilled in completeness without bitachon, and shows it in guarding the eyes in the street, in honesty in business, and in a yeshiva bochur's plans for his future. He describes the rising holiness of Hoshana Rabbah and Shemini Atzeres, urges using these days, and closes with a brachah for a good sealing.

catalogTitle: גודל מעלת קדושת הסוכה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the sukkah, Yaakov Avinu's gift to his children, carries the holiness of the Beis HaMikdash and the shelter of the Shechinah, and that from it a Jew takes bitachon, protection and simcha for the whole year.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Zohar's reading of 'betzilo chimadti veyashavti' as the sukkah, the shade of emunah under the wings of the Shechinah, which carries the holiness of Eretz Yisrael and of the Beis HaMikdash. He traces the sukkah to Yaakov Avinu and shows that each Yom Tov gives its own gift: Pesach gives emunah, Sukkos gives bitachon, a higher level. Through the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva, the Rambam, the Divrei Chaim and the Rokeach, he shows that the sukkah's shelter goes with a person wherever he goes. He explains why the sukkah, like Noach's teivah and the Mishkan, is built by measurements, and illustrates bitachon with Chizkiyahu sleeping while Sanheriv besieged Yerushalayim. He ties bitachon to simcha, gives practical applications, and closes with the sukkah as a place of renewed judgment and of chassadim.

en: Sitting in the sukkah is sitting in the shade of emunah, under the wings of the Shechinah, and one should have this in mind while sitting there.
The sukkah carries the holiness of Eretz Yisrael and, according to tzaddikim, of the Beis HaMikdash.
Each Yom Tov has its own gift: from Pesach one takes emunah and from Sukkos, the Yom Tov of Yaakov Avinu, one takes bitachon, a higher level than emunah.
Once a person has made the sukkah his dwelling, its protection goes with him even when he steps out, and he takes it along for the whole year.
Simcha comes from bitachon: one who feels secure in Hashem can truly rejoice, which is why Sukkos is the time of our joy.
Bitachon must be lived in practice: in unhurried davening, in guarding the eyes, and in not interrupting learning for business.
