Tisha B'Av and the rebuilding of Yerushalayim
Amalek and the tribe of Dan

title.en: Building malchus from Rosh Hashanah to Shemini Atzeres

summary.en: The Rav opens with 'vayiven Hashem Elokim es hatzela' and explains that beneath its plain meaning lies the building of malchus, the kallah Knesses Yisroel, renewed each year from Rosh Hashanah to Shemini Atzeres. Shemini Atzeres is the center around which all the festivals turn.

title.en: What is called a kallah

summary.en: The Rav lists the things called a kallah, all bound to the attribute of malchus: the Torah, Shabbos, Yerushalayim, the Mishkan and Beis Hamikdash, and the esrog. On Shemini Atzeres 'od evneich venivneis' is fulfilled, and since a wedding needs preparation, that preparation starts on Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Mourning on Tisha B'Av builds Yerushalayim

summary.en: In the name of Rabbi Mordechai of Lechovitch, the Rav says Tisha B'Av, Elul and the Yamim Noraim prepare for Simchas Torah, and the mourning itself begins the building of Yerushalayim, illustrated by the story of Napoleon. He then brings the Gemara that the Torah has seven books, making Devarim the seventh, the kallah.

title.en: Sefer Devarim as the kallah and the esrog

summary.en: The Rav explains that Devarim stands between the Written and the Oral Torah, and that after the seven nechamos the kallah goes to the chuppah on Rosh Hashanah. Devarim is begun on Shabbos Chazon and finished on Simchas Torah; like the esrog, the seventh of the species, it is set apart, which Rabbeinu Bachya sees in its not beginning with a vav.

title.en: Separation and reunion: the joy of a wedding

summary.en: The Rav asks why the esrog and Devarim must be set apart, and answers from Chavah taken from Adam's side: the Chiddushei HaRim says the joy of a wedding is the reunion of parts that were separated. The avodah of Sukkos is to bring the esrog close to the lulav, Knesses Yisroel to Hashem, which is also the idea of teshuvah.

title.en: Yerushalayim, Devarim and the completed moon

summary.en: From the Ba'al HaTanya's words on mourning at chatzos, the Rav explains that weeping over Yerushalayim, the heart of Knesses Yisroel, builds it, and that learning Devarim is a sefer of teshuvah. He then compares the kallah to the moon, covered by clouds that the shofar scatters on Rosh Hashanah, and made whole on Shemini Atzeres.

title.en: Why Simchas Torah continues with Bereishis

summary.en: The Rav says the building of the kallah ends on Shemini Atzeres, when one embraces the Torah as a kallah. Yet the reading continues into Bereishis until 'vayechulu', because the world lacked menuchah: Shabbos, the kallah, was the completing creation, and the tenth maamar, according to Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen, is the creation of woman.

title.en: Devarim, the esrog and Shlomo's wedding

summary.en: The Rav brings Rabbeinu Bachya that Devarim corresponds to the esrog and the last hei of Hashem's name, and the Chasam Sofer on why the brachah is made on the lulav. He cites Rebbe Reb Bunim and Rabbi Pinchas of Koretz that Shemini Atzeres is the wedding of Shlomo HaMelech, and reads the hei of 'liShlomo' with Rashi on 'ohalo'.

title.en: Praising the kallah from the feet up

summary.en: The Rav notes that in Shir Hashirim the chassan is praised from head to feet, while the kallah is praised from the feet upward, beginning 'ma yafu fe'amayich'. He explains that Knesses Yisroel has a head, heart, hands and feet, both within each generation and across the generations, from the generation of the desert down to the heel before Moshiach.

title.en: The trials of the last generation

summary.en: The Rav describes the present generation as the heel: once Jews were kept apart in the ghettos, today the walls are broken and the Satan, fighting for his existence, brings daily new inventions such as cellphones, computers and the internet, and many have fallen. Yet those who hold on are climbing smooth walls, and that is why Shlomo begins the kallah's praise from the feet.

title.en: Amalek, the tribe of Dan and Shimshon

summary.en: The Rav explains that Amalek attacked the stragglers, the tribe of Dan who were left outside the clouds of glory, because he envies the acharis of the Jew, as with Haman at the end of the Babylonian exile. He shows that Dan is where faults appear, yet Hashem always pairs Dan with Yehudah: Shimshon, whose mother was from Yehudah, Betzalel and Oholiav, Shlomo and Chiram; Yehudah is fire and alacrity, Dan is dust and sluggishness.

title.en: Bikkurim, Shimshon's hair and our generation

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the early fig of bikkurim, alacrity brought to Yerushalayim, with the late one, Dan. He explains why Shimshon's strength lay in his hair: hair is the last thing formed in a person, the aspect of Dan and of the last generation. The task of this generation, he says, is not to let its hair be shorn, not to be drawn after the internet and cellphones.

title.en: Shimshon's prayer for our generation

summary.en: The Rav explains the name Delilah from the Gemara in Sotah, and says this generation's beauty is that it fights Amalek tooth and nail. Shimshon, who knew his soul would return in the sparks of our generation, prayed 'zochreini na vechazkeini na ach hapa'am' for us, and the Rav says a Jew should say this prayer at every trial.

title.en: The sukkah as a shield in a time of fear

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that a generation strengthened in the mitzvah of sukkah is shielded by it, at a time when the world fears Iran, which he identifies with Paras. He cites the Midrash on the year Moshiach is revealed and the king of Paras provokes the world, when Hashem tells Israel not to fear, and says that sitting in the sukkah with joy shields all of Klal Yisroel.

title.en: Simchas Torah: the joy of the simple Jew

summary.en: The Rav explains that the last generations are the end of the Torah, where Moshe's passing brought forgetting of halachos, yet on Simchas Torah one rejoices there because it is joined at once to Bereishis: every Jew will have a tikkun. He brings the Ba'al HaTanya's siddur that Simchas Beis Hashoeva is the joy of talmidei chachamim while Simchas Torah is the joy of the simple Jew, and closes with brachos for the year.

catalogTitle: הקמת קומת המלכות - יחוד קודשא בריך הוא ושכינתי'

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that malchus means bittul to Hashem, shows how Shlomo HaMelech embodied it as a foretaste of Moshiach, and presents Shemini Atzeres as the day of the complete union of Hashem and the Shechinah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Tishrei as the seventh month, the time of malchus, and asks why Hashem was angry when the Jews requested a king, although appointing one is a mitzvah. Malchus, he explains, means bittul: like the moon that has no light of its own, holiness is measured by self-nullification, while the kelipah says 'I am something'. Following the Tzemach Tzedek, a true king is himself batel to Hashem and becomes the bridge that brings malchus shamayim to the people. Malchus has a soul (the king), a place (the Beis HaMikdash) and a time (Tishrei). Shlomo HaMelech, who ruled the whole world, built the Mikdash, instituted eruvin and netilas yadayim and married Pharaoh's daughter to subdue the kelipah, was a sample of the days of Moshiach. The work from Tisha b'Av to Shemini Atzeres is to turn Yirmiyahu back into Shlomo, and Shemini Atzeres is the point of complete yichud.

en: Malchus means bittul: the more a person nullifies himself to Hashem, the more holiness he has, while the kelipah is the sense of being something.
The purpose of a Jewish king is not to fight wars but to be batel to Hashem and to bring malchus shamayim upon the people, as a bridge between them and Hashem.
Malchus has a soul, a place and a time: the king, the Beis HaMikdash and the month of Tishrei.
Shlomo HaMelech, who brought malchus shamayim to the whole world, was a temporary sample of the days of Moshiach.
Shlomo's institutions of eruvin and netilas yadayim both express bittul: making the world one reshus hayachid and raising all one's powers to Hashem.
The work from Tisha b'Av to Shemini Atzeres is to turn churban into binyan, and Shemini Atzeres is the peak of the yichud of Hashem and the Shechinah.

title.en: Tishrei, malchus and the mitzvah of a king

summary.en: The Rav opens with Tishrei as the seventh month, the time of accepting malchus shamayim, and introduces the mitzvah of appointing a king. He asks why Hashem was angry when the people asked Shmuel for a king, and notes that the Gemara links three mitzvos upon entering the land: a king, wiping out Amalek and building the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Malchus as bittul, from the moon to the Akeidah

summary.en: The Rav explains, following the Tanya, that malchus means bittul, like the moon that has no light of its own, and that kedushah grows with bittul while the kelipah is 'yesh'. He describes the hidden love in every Jew that surfaces in mesiras nefesh at Shema, the Avos as a merkavah, and Avraham Avinu setting aside a new, supernatural love for Yitzchak at the Akeidah.

title.en: The king as a bridge; the three mitzvos of the land

summary.en: Citing the Tzemach Tzedek, the Rav explains that a true king is batel to Hashem and through him the people become batel, which is how he reads 'Hashem Elokeichem malkechem'. He then explains the three mitzvos of entering Eretz Yisrael, the place of malchus: a king, destroying Amalek as the kelipah of 'yesh', and the Beis HaMikdash as the place of prostration, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar on why the Girgashi left the land.

title.en: Soul, place and time of malchus

summary.en: The Rav lays out malchus in olam, shanah and nefesh: the king who bows through all of Shemoneh Esrei and is warned not to raise his heart, Tishrei when Jews prostrate themselves, and the Beis HaMikdash. He then introduces a higher level of king who brings malchus shamayim to the whole world, Moshiach.

title.en: Shlomo HaMelech, a sample of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav presents Shlomo HaMelech as a king over the whole world, the full moon after fifteen generations, and a sample of the days of Moshiach as the Rambam describes them; David's inner soul of Moshiach was revealed in his son. He describes Shlomo's unparalleled love of Hashem from the Zohar, his name Yedidyah, the Mikdash 'paved with love', and the Arizal's explanation of his many wives as a way to bring the nations under malchus shamayim.

title.en: Reshus hayachid: Shabbos and the danger of 'two'

summary.en: After gematrios linking Shlomo to 'Hashem malach', the Rav explains that true malchus shamayim means the world becoming a reshus hayachid. Shabbos, the day of malchus, centers on the melachah of carrying out to the reshus harabim; 'yom echad' versus the second day, when division and Gehinnom were created, explains the danger of zugos.

title.en: Eruvin, netilas yadayim and Pharaoh's daughter

summary.en: The Rav explains Shlomo's two institutions: eruvin turns a public domain into one reshus hayachid, and netilah means lifting the hands, like Rebbi raising his ten fingers at his passing. He then tells how Shlomo married Pharaoh's daughter on the night before the dedication of the Mikdash, overslept the tamid, and the decree of destruction followed, explaining that he had hoped to subdue the greatest kelipah.

title.en: Shlomo's name and his new anointing

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shlomo was so batel that he carries Hashem's own name, as Chazal say every Shlomo in Shir HaShirim is holy, and that his reign was a yichud shalem. He asks why Shlomo had to be anointed although he was a king's son, and answers that his was a new kind of malchus, the malchus of the days of Moshiach, not merely David's.

title.en: Ruth, the two women, and Moshiach in hiding

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Ruth lived to see Shlomo judge the two women, and retells that judgment. He explains that the line of David always came into the world in concealed, even unseemly ways (Lot's daughters, Yehudah and Tamar, the doubts about Ruth) so that the Satan would not notice, until Hashem's oath to David made it safe to reveal.

title.en: The two women as kelipah submitting

summary.en: Following the Arizal, the Rav identifies the two women as the chief kelipos, and explains that in kelipah the female is stronger, applying it to his own time. Their coming humbly to Shlomo for judgment was the submission of kelipah to kedushah, a sample of Moshiach, and this was the consolation Boaz offered Ruth in her lowliness.

title.en: Betzalel, Shlomo and the yichud of Shemini Atzeres

summary.en: The Rav explains why the people had to consent to Betzalel through the Arizal's teaching that Shlomo was a spark of Betzalel, so building the Mishkan was an act of malchus. He then defines yichud Kudsha Brich Hu u'Shechinteih as Jews cleaving to Hashem, calls Shemini Atzeres the peak of that yichud, citing the Bnei Yissaschar, and brings the Lechovitcher that this work begins on Tisha b'Av, like a black background for a colorful bird.

title.en: From Yirmiyahu back to Shlomo

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer that Shlomo was reincarnated in Yirmiyahu, so the work from Tisha b'Av to Shemini Atzeres is to turn Yirmiyahu back into Shlomo. Shemini Atzeres is a sample of Moshiach that does not belong to this world, with Shlomo as its guest, and Sefer Devarim, following the Arizal and Rabbeinu Bachya, corresponds to the final heh and to the esrog.

title.en: Sefer Devarim from Shabbos Chazon to Simchas Torah

summary.en: The Rav notes that Sefer Devarim is begun on Shabbos Chazon and completed on Shemini Atzeres, and describes a Jew's task in these months as turning Eichah into Shir HaShirim and churban into binyan, rebuilding the Jerusalem in his heart through teshuvah. He links the king's reading of Devarim at Hakhel, the Mishnah of Tu b'Av about King Shlomo, and the day of union between Hashem and Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Shemini Atzeres, the point, and answering amen

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shemini Atzeres is not called a 'chag', a circle, but is the point at the center, Hashem Himself, and laments that people hardly speak of it. He brings that on this day one may ask of Hashem, as Shlomo was told 'ask', describes the simple Jews dancing and every Jew's aliyah to the last letters of the Torah, and urges answering amen with kavanah, closing with a tefillah for a world that is entirely Shemini Atzeres.

catalogTitle: “מי לה' אלי” - מסירת נפש ע"י דביקות בה'

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah was won through the mesiras nefesh of the Chashmonaim's cry 'Mi laHashem elai', and that every Jew can renew it each year by giving up pieces of his own will for Hashem, especially in the confusing times before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that of all the mitzvos, Chanukah is built on mesiras nefesh: the Chashmonaim went to a war that could not be won by nature, after the cry 'Mi laHashem elai', which repeats the mesiras nefesh of Shevet Levi at the Golden Calf. Each year the same light returns, and the mitzvos and minhagim of Chanukah are the means to receive it. Mesiras nefesh, he explains, does not only mean dying; nefesh means will, and giving up one's will for Hashem, even in small daily pieces, is mesiras nefesh. Routine Yiddishkeit is not yet avodas Hashem. Through the Rambam on Shevet Levi he teaches that anyone who devotes himself to Hashem becomes like Levi, with Hashem as his portion. Chanukah comes in the darkest time, like the 'erev' of confusion before Moshiach, whose test, like Avraham's Akeidah, is emunah.

en: Of all the mitzvos, Chanukah was earned through mesiras nefesh, in a war the Chashmonaim could not win by nature.
The cry 'Mi laHashem elai' of the Chashmonaim repeats the mesiras nefesh of Shevet Levi at the Golden Calf, and it repeats itself every year on Chanukah.
Nefesh means a person's will, so mesiras nefesh means giving up one's will for Hashem, and small daily acts of it can add up to more than giving one's life once.
Routine Yiddishkeit, done out of habit, is not yet avodas Hashem; avodas Hashem means bending one's will to the Ribono shel Olam.
According to the Rambam, not only Shevet Levi but any person who devotes himself to Hashem becomes holy, with Hashem as his portion and inheritance.
The time before Moshiach is an 'erev', a time of mixture and confusion, and its great test is emunah, like Avraham's last test at the Akeidah.

title.en: Chanukah built on mesiras nefesh

summary.en: After a garbled opening, the Rav says that Chanukah, more than any mitzvah, came from mesiras nefesh: the Chashmonaim cried 'Mi laHashem elai' and went to a war they could not win by nature. He brings the Rambam that ner Chanukah is a very dear mitzvah, says the same lights return every year, and ties the Chashmonaim to Shevet Levi at the Golden Calf.

title.en: Preparing to receive the Chanukah light

summary.en: The Rav explains that the lighting and the other mitzvos and minhagim of Chanukah are the means Chazal gave to become vessels for its light. He notes that people in the world give themselves over to all kinds of ideologies, and says how much more a Jew should identify with 'Mi laHashem elai' and be ready for the mesiras nefesh his time demands.

title.en: Nefesh means will

summary.en: The Rav explains that mesiras nefesh does not only mean being killed; from 'im yesh es nafshechem' he shows that nefesh means will, so giving up one's will for Hashem is mesiras nefesh. He says routine Yiddishkeit is not avodas Hashem, and that a whole day of small pieces of mesiras nefesh can be greater than giving one's life once.

title.en: The prince and the broken stone

summary.en: The Rav brings a mashal from the seforim of a king's son sentenced to be killed by a heavy stone dropped on him; since the law could not be changed, the stone was broken into small pieces and thrown at him one by one, and he lived. So, he says, a Jew's daily efforts against his own will, in davening and the like, add up to great mesiras nefesh.

title.en: Connection to the tzaddik and giving something up

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban that Moshe counted the Jews so each would have contact with him and his brachos, and says a Jew's success depends on his connection to the tzaddik. He tells of a Jew who came to the Chiddushei HaRim leaning on a cane, and concludes that each person must take on, according to his level, to give something of himself away; keeping the 'cane' in hand is not readiness.

title.en: Chanukah and the penimiyus of a Jew

summary.en: The Rav cites a tradition handed down from the Ba'al Shem Tov through the Maggid of Mezritch that on Chanukah one can receive the inner dimension, the penimiyus. He explains that the innermost point of every Jew is revealed through Chanukah and mesiras nefesh. The rest of this stretch is too garbled to follow.

title.en: Every Jew can become like Shevet Levi

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that Shevet Levi received no portion in the land because it was set apart to serve Hashem, and that any person who devotes himself this way becomes holy and Hashem is his portion, as David HaMelech said though he was not a Levi. He contrasts people who pour all their energy into parnassah with one who looks up to the Ribono shel Olam as his inheritance, and asks each person on Chanukah to give Hashem a larger share of his time and strength.

title.en: Light in the darkness of 'erev'

summary.en: The Rav says Chanukah comes in the darkest part of the year and brings a little light of the Ribono shel Olam into that darkness. He explains that 'erev' is a time of mixture when things cannot be told apart, while 'boker' comes from examining, and says the world now stands in such an 'erev' before Moshiach, when everything is tested and one must strengthen emunah.

title.en: Lighting from within

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the mitzvah to light outside, when the Jewish home was full of light that shone into the street, with today, when the 'outside' has come into the home. Now one must light from within and bring the light of Torah and love of Torah inside. Our menoros are dearer to us than the more attractive lights of the street because of the mesiras nefesh behind them.

title.en: Avraham's first and last tests

summary.en: The Rav compares Avraham's first test, letting himself be thrown into the fire of Ur Kasdim for a G-d he had recognized himself, with his last, the Akeidah, after Hashem had promised him offspring through Yitzchak. He brings from Breslov that before Moshiach the main test will be emunah, and the Ramban that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, so the Akeidah corresponds to the last test before Moshiach.

title.en: 'Kach na': the last test of emunah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that 'kach na' is a request: Hashem asked Avraham to stand the last test so the earlier ones would not be called empty, and says Hashem asks the same of Jews today in the test of confusion, warning against reading heresy. He speaks of simple emunah without cheshbonos, and of emunah and tzedakah as what brings Moshiach; the end of the recording is garbled.

catalogTitle: The Greatness and Downfall of זמרי בן סלוא and how it Corresponds to חודש אב

oneLiner.en: The Rav traces the three names of the Nasi of Shimon, Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai, Shaul ben haKenaanis and Zimri ben Salu, as his greatness, his fall and his coming tikkun, and shows how they correspond to the month of Av, the month of Shimon.

abstract.en: On the hilulah of the Arizal, the Rav opens with the Arizal's teaching of gilgul: Hashem ensures that no neshama is ever lost. He turns to Parshas Pinchas, read as Av is blessed, and to Zimri ben Salu, who had three names. As Shaul ben haKenaanis he carried an impurity inherited from Dinah; as Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai he was the great Nasi of Shimon. The Arizal reveals that Zimri returned as Rabbi Akiva and Kozbi as the wife of Turnus Rufus. Since the months correspond to the tribes and Av is the month of Shimon, Av follows the same path: great, fallen, and destined to become a joyous Yom Tov. The Rav then explains Rabbi Akiva's laughter at the fox on the Har HaBayis: the fox, shual, was Shaul ben haKenaanis, part of his own neshama coming to its tikkun. The ayin of galus will turn into an aleph, and the Rav ends that now, close to the Geulah, is the time to lift up Av.

en: According to the Arizal's teaching of gilgul, Hashem brings every neshama back again and again until it reaches its perfection, so that no one is ever lost.
Zimri ben Salu had three names, Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai, Shaul ben haKenaanis and Zimri ben Salu, each marking a period of his greatness or his fall.
Zimri's fall came from an impurity inherited from Dinah, who was violated by Shechem; his essence remained pure.
The twelve months correspond to the twelve tribes, and Av, the fifth month, is the month of Shimon, whose Nasi was Zimri.
When Mashiach comes, Av will be a month of joy and Tisha B'Av will be like Shemini Atzeres and Simchas Torah.
Rabbi Akiva laughed at the fox in the Kodesh HaKodashim because he saw in it Shaul ben haKenaanis, a part of his own neshama coming to its tikkun.
The Rav says the Geulah seems very close, and now is the time to work hard to lift Av from the ground to where it belongs.

title.en: The Arizal and the secret of gilgul

summary.en: On the hilulah of the Arizal, the Rav compares the Torah to a garden with gems hidden below its surface, and explains that one pillar of the Arizal's teaching is gilgul: Hashem devises ways so that no neshama is ever lost.

title.en: Shaul ben haKenaanis: the source of Zimri's fall

summary.en: The Rav introduces Zimri ben Salu and his three names, and explains the name Shaul ben haKenaanis: Zimri lent himself to sin because of an impurity inherited from Dinah, though his essence was pure.

title.en: Shelumiel's lost name and the Arizal's gilgulim

summary.en: As Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai he was the great Nasi of Shimon; when he fell, Pinchas took the name of Shakai and became Eliyahu, the angel of the bris. The Rav then brings the Arizal that Zimri returned as Rabbi Akiva and Kozbi as the wife of Turnus Rufus, and links the 24,000 who died to Rabbi Akiva's 24,000 students.

title.en: Av is the month of Shimon

summary.en: The Rav explains that the twelve months correspond to the twelve tribes in the order of the Nesiim's offerings, so Av is the month of Shimon, whose Nasi bore all three names, and he describes Av as a sorrowful month.

title.en: The future greatness of Av

summary.en: Rather than the mourning of Av, the Rav speaks of its greatness: Zechariah's promise that the fasts will become days of joy, and the sefarim's comparison of the three weeks to the days from Rosh Hashanah to Simchas Torah. He describes Zimri's original greatness as Nasi, whose day in Nisan is still a Yom Tov, ties Shimon to Nisan, and brings the Medrash that Mashiach is born on Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Rabbi Akiva laughs at the fox

summary.en: The Rav tells the Gemara at the end of Makkos: the Tannaim wept at a fox leaving the Kodesh HaKodashim while Rabbi Akiva laughed, since the fulfilled prophecy of destruction assures the prophecy of comfort. He notes the Rambam's view that the place keeps its holiness, and asks why the Gemara stresses the wording of their reply.

title.en: Everything has its place; Rabbi Akiva's two laughs

summary.en: Bringing the Maharal that everything has its place according to its neshama, the Rav asks what the fox was doing in the Kodesh HaKodashim. He compares Rabbi Akiva's laughter at the wife of Turnus Rufus, whom he foresaw would convert and become his wife, and concludes that the fox too was part of Rabbi Akiva's neshama: shual is Shaul ben haKenaanis.

title.en: The fox, the vineyard and Akiva nichamtanu

summary.en: The fox stands for the zenus that destroys the vineyard of Jewish purity, the sin of Zimri; seeing it in the Kodesh HaKodashim, the place of atonement, Rabbi Akiva saw Zimri's tikkun beginning. The Rav adds that shual is the gematria of Zimri ben Salu and 'Akiva nichamtanu' the gematria of Kozbi bas Tzur.

title.en: From ayin to aleph

summary.en: The Rav shows that an ayin turning into an aleph marks a tikkun: the suspended ayin of 'chazir miyaar', and Rabbi Meir's 'kasnos or' with an aleph. With the Chasam Sofer he explains that galus always carries the ayin of seventy, and that Shaul only lent himself to sin and did not sell his neshama.

title.en: Shimon will rise: the future of Av

summary.en: The Rav sums up: Shimon was great, fell, began to rise through Rabbi Akiva, and will fully rise when Tisha B'Av becomes a Yom Tov. Adam's garment of skin will become a garment of light, the gematria of Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai, and he ends that the Geulah seems close and now is the time to work hard to lift up Av.

catalogTitle: ביאור על מאמר חז”ל “פתילות ושמנים שאין מדליקין בהם בשבת מדליקין בהם בחנוכה”

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah, won by the holy boldness of Aharon's descendants against Yavan, reveals the essential bond between Hashem and the Jewish people that no darkness or sin can break, which is why even 'wicks and oils' unfit for Shabbos can be lit on Chanukah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Aharon's distress at being left out of the nesi'im's offerings at the dedication of the mizbe'ach, which the nesi'im brought with a certain boldness. Yavan, the leopard in Daniel's vision, embodies brazenness, and its decree that the Jews write on the ox's horn that they have no share in the G-d of Israel rested on the sin of the golden calf. Aharon, bashful by nature, was told his time would come: his descendants, the Chashmonaim, would use holy boldness to defeat Yavan. The Rav explains that the Jewish bond with Hashem is essential, like a wife's sense that her husband lives, and this is the trait of Levi, who did not serve the calf. Chanukah shows that this bond remains even in darkness, which is why wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah. The recording then continues with teachings on not seeing Hashem's whole plan, a story, and the power of a Jewish psak.

en: Yavan, the leopard of Daniel's vision, embodies brazenness, and the Jews' victory over it meant taking that boldness as spoil and sanctifying it.
Aharon, who was bashful, held back from the nesi'im's offering, and was consoled that his descendants the Chashmonaim would serve Hashem with holy boldness against Yavan.
The Greeks claimed through the 'horn of the ox', the golden calf, that the Jews had lost their bond with Hashem; Chanukah shows that the bond is essential and never breaks.
Sensing the essential bond is the trait of shevet Levi, who did not serve the calf, and Chanukah and Levi are therefore 'one thing'.

Wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah, hinting that souls that cannot shine through Shabbos can be lit by Chanukah, whose light reaches below ten tefachim into the place of the kelipos.
Chanukah is not a commemoration of the past: the closer the generations come to Moshiach, the more its light is revealed.
What Jews decide according to the Torah below is followed in Heaven, which is why Dovid HaMelech insisted on ruling himself.

title.en: Aharon and the nesi'im's offerings

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Avnei Nezer and with Aharon's distress that neither he nor his tribe took part in the nesi'im's offerings at the dedication of the mizbe'ach, noting the Ramban that Hashem's answer hints at the Chanukah lights. He brings the Midrash on 'I ate my honeycomb with my honey': the nesi'im brought a chatas and ketores, which are never brought voluntarily, yet Hashem accepted them out of love for Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Yavan the leopard and brazenness

summary.en: The Rav explains that in Daniel's vision Yavan is the third beast, the leopard, whose trait is boldness, and describes the Greek decree to write on the ox's horn that the Jews have no share in the G-d of Israel. Victory means taking the spoil, so the Jews sanctified boldness; he connects this to the tzitz worn on the forehead and says boldness may be used only for Hashem's service against scoffers.

title.en: Copper, the forehead and Aharon's shame

summary.en: Continuing from the Avnei Nezer, the Rav links the four metals to the four kingdoms, with copper standing for the boldness of Yavan, as in 'your forehead is copper'. He brings Rashi that Aharon was ashamed to approach the mizbe'ach and was told 'for this you were chosen', and explains that Aharon was the opposite of boldness.

title.en: Aharon's time: the Chashmonaim's holy boldness

summary.en: The Rav explains that Aharon held back from the nesi'im's offering out of modesty, and Hashem told him his time would come when his descendants, the Chashmonaim, would fight Yavan with holy boldness and win Chanukah. He applies this to dark times, when a Jew must strengthen himself with boldness and shine even 'outside', and explains that because the Jews kept the chukim they merited the light of Torah and the flowering of the Oral Torah.

title.en: The ox's horn and the essential bond

summary.en: Returning to a piece of the Avnei Nezer, the Rav explains that the 'ox' in the Greek decree is the golden calf: the Greeks argued that since the Jews served it, they have no bond with Hashem. He describes the bond of Israel to Hashem as that of wife and husband, and explains the halachah of a woman who remarried on a report of her husband's death: a wife truly bound to her husband would sense that he is alive.

title.en: Shevet Levi, maaser and the tenth point

summary.en: The Rav explains that sensing the essential bond is the trait of Levi, who did not fall at the calf and whose name comes from 'this time my husband will be joined to me'. Levi is the maaser, the inner point in every Jew, so a bas Levi who did not sense her husband was alive loses the right to maaser; he adds that a minyan of ten reveals this same point, so that ten resha'im make a minyan and nine tzaddikim do not.

title.en: Chanukah and Levi are one

summary.en: The Rav returns to Aharon's consolation, 'yours is greater than theirs', and explains that the Chanukah of the Chashmonaim answers the Greeks' claim: Levi and Chanukah both show the eternal bond of Israel with Hashem, which remains even in churban. He explains why Chanukah has no festive meal: it is the hidden essential bond, which the Beis HaMikdash service did not display.

title.en: Chanukah grows as Moshiach nears

summary.en: The Rav notes that the Mishnah hardly mentions Chanukah and the Gemara gives it only a few pages, while from the Arizal and the Ba'al Shem Tov onward it was greatly expanded, because the closer to Moshiach the more its light is revealed, like the darkest hour before dawn. He explains the phrase 'the eight days of Chanukah' as one long weekday festival that stretches into Teves, in the darkest time of the year.

title.en: Lighting in the dark: tefillah, hiddur, gazing

summary.en: The Rav says that when it is dark a Jew must feel the bond with Hashem, and calls Chanukah our war in exile, fought like the Chashmonaim with tefillah. He urges praying at the lights for children who are talmidei chachamim, beautifying the mitzvah with a fine, clean menorah, and sitting by the lights to look at them, since every Jew is himself a Chanukah light and from them one draws the light of Torah for the whole year.

title.en: Wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings the statement that wicks and oils which may not be lit on Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah, and the sefarim that souls which cannot be lit through Shabbos can be lit on Chanukah, whose light is placed below ten tefachim to reach the place of the kelipos. He brings Rebbe Tzadok HaKohen that the alphabetical chapters of Tehillim end with an extra verse of redemption beyond the order, showing that Hashem never lets a Jew be lost, and that the light of Moshiach is revealed on Chanukah.

title.en: Raising lost souls; Shabbos Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav says that a Jew who lights proclaims the opposite of the Greeks' cry, that he does have a share in the G-d of Israel, and that the Chanukah light raises lost souls from among the kelipos, the sparks of Moshiach ben David and Moshiach ben Yosef. He calls Shabbos Chanukah the essence of Chanukah, notes that this year's Chanukah begins and ends with Shabbos as a hint of Moshiach, and discusses lighting on erev Shabbos before dark.

title.en: Rising at Kedushah and Krias Shema

summary.en: The Rav explains the custom of rising on the toes at 'kadosh' in Kedushah: when Jews say Kedushah, even the lower angels rise to the level of the higher ones, and the person rises with them. He adds that at Krias Shema the love of Hashem is awakened, and the animal soul itself, whose root is in the holy beasts of the Divine chariot, joins in song.

title.en: Not seeing the whole picture

summary.en: Mentioning Shabbos Mevarchim Adar, the Rav speaks of simple emunah that Hashem runs the world even when it is not seen, bringing the Gemara that the Jews of Mordechai's time were punished for attending Achashverosh's feast, and Yaakov's sending of Yosef that led to the exile in Egypt. He applies this to the chevlei Moshiach and the six million, citing the Satmar Rebbe that they will return to see the building of the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Two kvitlach and the moment of birth

summary.en: The Rav tells of a Rebbe who received two kvitlach at once, one for a woman in difficult labor and one for a dying man, and explained that the dying man's soul had to enter the child. From here he discusses hastening births by medical means, explaining that each child is to be born at a moment and mazal set in Heaven, and that we cannot understand the paths of gilgulim.

title.en: Judgment beside the mizbe'ach; Heaven follows beis din

summary.en: The Rav explains why the laws of judgment are placed beside the mizbe'ach: the body comes from the place of the mizbe'ach, and the death sentence of beis din is itself a tikkun. He brings Rabbeinu Gershom, whose takanos were accepted in Heaven, and the Midrash on the Mishkan as a pledge, concluding that whatever Jews rule by the Torah is followed above, and that the avodah of Adar is to reveal Hashem's hidden guidance.

title.en: Why Dovid HaMelech ruled himself

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Dovid HaMelech busied himself at night with questions of purity to permit a wife to her husband, and consulted Mefiboshes. He asks why the king needed to rule at all, and answers that Dovid's soul reached Atzilus and he was king of all Israel, so his ruling affected all the worlds and the bond of Klal Yisrael with Hashem.

title.en: Moshe's judges and the Maggid's question

summary.en: The Rav brings Moshe Rabbeinu's rebuke about the appointment of judges and Rashi that the Jews should have wanted to learn from Moshe himself. He tells that the Maggid asked his talmidim who is the tzaddik of the generation and they were silent; had they answered, it would have been accepted in Heaven, since beis din below rules and the court above follows.

catalogTitle: טומאה היא כלי זיין של יון במלחמתו כנגד אמונה וטהרה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah comes from the 'eighth', the world above nature and the light of Moshiach, so its oil can reach and free even the Jews whom Shabbos cannot lift.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a teaching of early Chassidic sefarim: oils that may not be lit on Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah, and so too there are Jews whom Shabbos cannot kindle but Chanukah can. Shabbos demands that a person rise to it, while on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down to the lowly, like a great man visiting the sick. Through the Maharal he explains that Chanukah comes from the Kodesh HaKodashim and from the number eight, which stands above the seven of nature, like milah, the Torah and the days of Moshiach. He contrasts shemitah, which frees an ordinary slave, with yovel, which frees even the slave who chose to stay, and wine of Shabbos kiddush with the oil of Chanukah. He then shows how parshas Vayeshev, with Yehuda and Yosef, carries the light of Moshiach, links Yevamos, Eruvin and Nidah to Moshiach, and closes by urging every Jew to take on Torah and teshuvah this Chanukah.

en: Oils unfit for Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah; likewise Jews whom Shabbos cannot kindle can be kindled by Chanukah.
Shabbos requires a Jew to raise himself to it, while on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down below ten tefachim to the Jew in exile.
Seven is the order of nature and eight is above it; Chanukah, from the Kodesh HaKodashim, belongs to the eighth.
Shemitah frees an ordinary slave, but only yovel, the 'eighth', frees the slave who chose to remain; Chanukah is of yovel.
Lighting the Chanukah candles reveals the light of Moshiach, as the Bnei Yissaschar writes.
Parshas Vayeshev is a Chanukah and Moshiach parsha: from Yehuda's descent comes Moshiach ben Dovid, and from Yosef's righteousness Moshiach ben Yosef.
The Rav says a Jew's whole life must be devoted to bringing Moshiach.

title.en: Oils unfit for Shabbos, kindled on Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav brings the early Chassidic sefarim: as oils unfit for Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah, Chanukah can kindle Jews whom Shabbos cannot. Shabbos demands rising up, while on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down, like a great man visiting the sick; he asks what in Chanukah makes this possible.

title.en: The Maharal: Chanukah from the Kodesh HaKodashim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Maharal: the miracle lasted eight days because it came from the Kodesh HaKodashim, where the Greeks had no rule. Seven is nature and eight is above it, as seen in milah on the eighth day, the Torah given after seven weeks, and the eightfold psalm of Torah.

title.en: The eighth: Moshiach, motzaei shevi'is and yovel

summary.en: The Rav shows that the eighth belongs to Moshiach: the harp of eight strings, Moshiach coming after the shemitah year, the melaveh malkah of Dovid HaMelech and the songs of Eliyahu on motzaei Shabbos. He tells how the Bnei Yissaschar learned the source of his soul from the Chozeh of Lublin, and brings his teaching that the Chanukah lights reveal the light of Moshiach.

title.en: Shemitah and yovel; wine and oil

summary.en: The Rav distinguishes the Shabbos of seven, shemitah, which frees an ordinary slave, from the great Shabbos of eight, yovel, which frees even the slave who stayed attached to his master. Shabbos is sanctified with wine, of the world of seven, while Chanukah is sanctified with oil, of the eighth; Chanukah is a cable of yovel let down into the weekday exile.

title.en: Oil rises; Vayeshev and the parsha of Yehuda

summary.en: The Rav explains that oil always rises to the top, like fire, because it belongs to a higher world, the eighth. Vayeshev, read on the Shabbos of Chanukah, is a Moshiach parsha with two descents; the first, Yehuda's, is a parsha of sin, yet from it come Peretz and Moshiach ben Dovid.

title.en: Yosef's trials and Moshiach ben Yosef

summary.en: The Rav describes Yosef, a seventeen-year-old alone in Egypt, standing a year of the hardest trials in kedushas habris until the image of his father saved him. The two parshiyos are opposites, yet both bring Moshiach, ben Dovid and ben Yosef, as the Midrash says that while all were busy, Hashem was creating the light of Moshiach.

title.en: Eruvin, Nidah, Yevamos: the hardest masechtos

summary.en: The Rav explains why Eruvin, Nidah and Yevamos are the hardest masechtos: all three deal with the coming of Moshiach. Yevamos is the tikkun of souls, and yibum is found only in the family of malchus Beis Dovid; Eruvin turns a public domain into a private one, as the world will become a reshus hayachid; Nidah corresponds to exile. The Chanukah light set at the door brings this light into the public domain.

title.en: Thirty-six lights; Tamar; a year of ches

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the thirty-six Chanukah lights correspond to the thirty-six masechtos, the last being Nidah. He ties Tamar, daughter of a kohen gadol, to the Kodesh HaKodashim, and says tzaddikim considered a year ending in ches especially auspicious for Moshiach. He rejects the idea that the founding of the state was a geulah, citing the Rambam.

title.en: Taking on Torah and teshuvah this Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav says every Jew must have a share in bringing Moshiach, and that Chanukah is a final chance for those who have not completed their teshuvah since Tishrei. He calls on each Jew to take on, with joy and resolve, Torah, the thirty-six masechtos and teshuvah, as preparation for Shabbos Vayeshev and Chanukah.

catalogTitle: כל ימי התשובה נכללים בחנוכה והעבודה מתחיל מר"ח כסלו

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that the eight days of Chanukah include all 122 days of teshuvah from Rosh Chodesh Elul, and that the avodah of Chanukah already begins on Rosh Chodesh Kislev.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Chernobyler's vision of joy in Heaven and asks what is special about Rosh Chodesh Kislev. He brings the Gemara that tzaddikim are inscribed on Rosh Hashanah and beinonim wait until Yom Kippur, adds that those whose teshuvah is still lacking wait until Shemini Atzeres, and that even later ones have a chance until Zos Chanukah. Each stage is hinted in the parshiyos read at that time: Vayelech's 30 pesukim match the 30 days of tzaddikim and Haazinu's 52 the days until Shemini Atzeres. Following the Bnei Yissaschar, that Chanukah is like another Rosh Hashanah, he counts 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah, the same as the pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu. Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim, hinting at a past year whose 122 days were not used. Finally, through the Zohar on Shema and Baruch Shem, he shows that Chanukah begins on Rosh Chodesh Kislev.

en: Tzaddikim are inscribed on Rosh Hashanah, beinonim wait until Yom Kippur, those whose teshuvah is lacking wait until Shemini Atzeres, and even slower ones have until Zos Chanukah.
Every stage of the time of teshuvah is hinted in the Torah, in the parshiyos read around Rosh Hashanah.
From Rosh Chodesh Elul until Zos Chanukah there are 122 days, and the eight days of Chanukah include this whole period of teshuvah.
The Rav attributes the troubles of the past year to the 122 days of teshuvah that were given and not used.
The avodah of Chanukah begins on Rosh Chodesh Kislev, the 24 days before Chanukah corresponding to the 24 letters of Baruch Shem.

title.en: The stages of judgment until Zos Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Chernobyler who saw great joy in Heaven and asks what is special about Rosh Chodesh Kislev. He brings the Gemara that tzaddikim are inscribed on Rosh Hashanah and beinonim on Yom Kippur, adds that others wait until Shemini Atzeres, and that even later ones have until Zos Chanukah.

title.en: The days of teshuvah in the parshiyos

summary.en: The Rav says everything is hinted in the Torah and finds the stages of teshuvah in the parshiyos read around Rosh Hashanah: Vayelech's 30 pesukim for the 30 days of tzaddikim, and Haazinu's 52 for the 52 days until Shemini Atzeres.

title.en: Chanukah includes 122 days of teshuvah

summary.en: Bringing the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah is like another Rosh Hashanah, the Rav counts the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah, settles the varying length of Cheshvan with the Gemara's rule of an unspecified month, and arrives at 122 days, the same number as the pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu.

title.en: Ki Savo's 122 pesukim and the past year

summary.en: The Rav brings his son-in-law's observation that Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim and asks why. Through the Gemara that Ki Savo is read before Rosh Hashanah to end the year with its curses, he explains that it hints at the past year's 122 days, which were not used, and so accounts for that year's many troubles.

title.en: Chanukah begins on Rosh Chodesh Kislev

summary.en: Through the Zohar that accepting the yoke of Heaven requires Shema Yisrael with its 25 letters and Baruch Shem with its 24, the Rav explains that the 24 days from Rosh Chodesh Kislev are Baruch Shem and Chanukah is Shema, so Chanukah begins on Rosh Chodesh Kislev. He closes with the joy in Heaven over the power of teshuvah and wishes for a good Chanukah.

catalogTitle: דרוש נפלא על טעמי המקרא - Golus is Rooted in Geulah - (ט' באב שחל בשבת)

oneLiner.en: Through the rare cantillation notes on 'alpayim ba'amah', the Rav shows that the churban of Av is rooted in the geulah of Nissan, and that the scattering of galus and the forgotten neshamos of the gid hanasheh are meant to be gathered back.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the calendar's cycle of rising and falling, in which Tammuz and Av belong to Esav. He then asks why the rare cantillation notes karnei parah and yerach ben yomo appear only on 'alpayim ba'amah' in Parshas Masei. Building on the Midrash that the first day of Pesach fixes the day of Tisha B'Av, he shows that churban is rooted in geulah. Av draws from Nissan as Shimon drew from Yehuda; karnei parah, the segmented cow's horn, stands for Av's division, and yerach ben yomo for Nissan, whose every day is as fresh as Rosh Chodesh. The shofar, symbol of ingathering, unites the two. He then explains Yaakov's gift to Esav, the gid hanasheh and Dina's daughter Osnas as lost neshamos that will return, and closes with the strength of Shabbos when Tisha B'Av falls on it.

en: Because the first day of Pesach determines the day of the week of Tisha B'Av, the Rav concludes that the churban is rooted in the geulah and exists for its sake.
The month of Av, the month of Shimon, receives its blessing from Nissan, the month of Yehuda, just as Shimon received his portion in Eretz Yisrael from within Yehuda's.

Karnei parah, named for the segmented horn of a cow, represents the division of Av, while yerach ben yomo represents Nissan, whose every day stays as fresh as Rosh Chodesh; the second serves the first and prepares it for the birth of Mashiach.
The scattering of galus, hinted in the note pazer, has the inner purpose of gathering the lost sparks and neshamos from among the nations.
The gid hanasheh that Yaakov lost to Esav's angel stands for forgotten Jewish neshamos under Esav's rule, and Tisha B'Av is the day that corresponds to it.
When Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos, Shabbos pushes it away and hints at the time when the gid hanasheh will be healed and the lost neshamos will return to Yaakov.

title.en: The calendar's descent and two rare notes

summary.en: The Rav describes the rise and fall of the calendar year, with Tammuz and Av belonging to Esav and the slide down after Sivan. He then notes that the words 'alpayim ba'amah' in Parshas Masei carry two notes found nowhere else in the Torah, karnei parah and yerach ben yomo, and asks why.

title.en: Pesach fixes Tisha B'Av: churban rooted in geulah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash on Eichah that the first day of Pesach and Tisha B'Av fall on the same weekday, by the order of at-bash, and the Pri Tzaddik that a Pesach on Shabbos is a sign of a good year. He concludes that the churban is rooted in the geulah, as Yocheved was born on the way into Mitzrayim and Mashiach is born on Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Av receives from Nissan; the lion and the lamb

summary.en: Following the Bnei Yissaschar, the Rav matches the months to the tribes: Av is Shimon's month and Nissan is Yehuda's, and as Shimon's portion and blessing came through Yehuda, Av draws from Nissan. He adds that the mazal of Av, the lion, is rooted in chesed and in the mazal of Nissan, the lamb.

title.en: The seven pazers: scattering to gather

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the great Shabbosos of the three weeks and of the seven pazer notes in Parshas Beha'aloscha, read as the year slides down. Pazer means scattering, galus among the nations, but with its milui it equals kibbutz galuyos: the scattering is meant to gather the sparks and lost Jews, and it is answered by the seven haftaros of consolation.

title.en: Why a cow's horn is no shofar

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah that every shofar is valid except a cow's, and Abaye's reason that a cow's horn grows in segments and looks like several shofros. He explains that the shofar symbolizes the gathering of all Jews, while the cow's horn is division, like pazer, and so it hints at Av, whose churban came through baseless hatred.

title.en: Masei, the Shelah on Nissan, and 'ben yomo'

summary.en: The Rav shows that the first letters of 'Eleh masei bnei Yisrael' hint at the four exiles. He brings the Shelah that every day of Nissan is Rosh Chodesh, and explains the halachic term ben yomo, a vessel that absorbed within the day and is still fresh, calling Nissan a month that never goes stale.

title.en: Yerach ben yomo serves karnei parah

summary.en: The Rav identifies yerach ben yomo with Nissan and karnei parah with Av, and explains that Nissan serves Av, bringing unity into the month of division and preparing it for the birth of Mashiach. The shofar with its milui equals both notes together, and karnei parah equals David Melech Yisrael; this is read on the first Shabbos of Av to strengthen Jews weary of galus.

title.en: The migrash, fresh love, and the vessels of Midian

summary.en: The Rav explains that a migrash of two thousand amos is the outskirts where one is driven out, yet it stays within the techum of the city, and that Nissan shows Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael never going stale. He then asks why the Torah required kashering Midian's vessels even when not ben yomo, and answers that Bilam tried to make that love lose its freshness, so Midian's forbidden taste never goes stale.

title.en: Esav's share in time and Yaakov's gift

summary.en: After a short interruption, the Rav explains that the journeys exist in time as well as place: the three weeks belong to Esav, and Tisha B'Av is Esav's portion, a day of mourning. He brings Yaakov's gift to Esav and the Midrash that Yaakov's flocks were Jewish neshamos, so the animals that went to Esav stand for neshamos that stray into Esav's domain.

title.en: The gid hanasheh: forgotten neshamos

summary.en: The Rav explains that in the wrestle with Esav's angel Yaakov won but was injured in the thigh, which the seforim read as descendants lost to Esav. Nasheh means forgetting, so the gid hanasheh is the forgotten neshamos, of whom Tziyon says 'Hashem has forgotten me', and he gives a gematria linking those words to Menachem Av.

title.en: Dina, Shechem and Osnas

summary.en: The Rav shows that what happened symbolically with the angel happened in fact in Shechem: Dina was taken, yet Yaakov lost nothing. Dina's daughter Osnas, hidden in a thornbush and brought to Mitzrayim, became Yosef's wife and the mother of Mashiach ben Yosef, so a hidden spark of Mashiach was in Shechem.

title.en: Seven consolations; Tisha B'Av as the gid hanasheh

summary.en: The Rav explains that the seven haftaros of consolation answer the seven pazers and assure Knesses Yisrael it will not be forgotten, since the scattering was meant to add converts and gather the lost. He brings the Zohar that the 365 days match the 365 sinews and Tisha B'Av is the gid hanasheh, and a Midrash reading 'minchah yashivu' as the return of Yaakov's gift to Esav.

title.en: Shechem's hidden spark and Dina's destiny

summary.en: The Rav says that the Shechem episode had the purpose of pazer, to be scattered in order to bring back, and that Shechem ben Chamor equals in gematria 'haMelech haMashiach ben Yosef'. Dina was meant to be Yosef and was switched, so she was destined from birth to provide Yosef's match. Tisha B'Av, lost to Esav, will return as a festival, as Zechariah says.

title.en: Shabbos Tisha B'Av heals the gid hanasheh

summary.en: The Rav notes that the Shabbos zemiros about Edom end with a passuk of geulah, and explains that eating on Tisha B'Av is like eating the gid hanasheh. When Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos it hints at the time the gid hanasheh will be healed; so too Yaakov arrived 'shalem', healed, in Shechem, on Shabbos.

title.en: We are the lost neshamos; the strength of Shabbos Chazon

summary.en: The Rav says that all of us, even those who keep Shabbos, are lost neshamos compared with earlier generations, and that these weeks are a time to return to Yaakov's flocks with bitachon and emunah. He closes with the moon on Tisha B'Av, the vision of the third Beis HaMikdash on Shabbos Chazon, and the Shabbos that pushes away Esav's angel, ending with the passuk of the consolation of Tziyon.

catalogTitle: להתקשר בנרות חנוכה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that on Chanukah the Shechinah breaks its own rule and descends below ten tefachim, into the darkest time of the year, to rekindle even the most distant Jewish souls, and he urges every Jew to grab hold of the Chanukah light.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that the Shechinah never descends below ten tefachim, and notes that Chanukah is the exception: its lights belong below ten. Chanukah is a weekday Yom Tov, and its light is kindled before the Shabbos lights and rises into them. He explains that the months of Teves and Shevas remained in the domain of the sitra achra; tekufas Teves, the longest night, was a day of idolatry since Adam HaRishon, and it was the day of Yosef's great test. Yet the Chanukah miracle came at that very time, for the Shechinah descends to souls in the 'public domain'. Ner, pesilah and shemen spell neshamah, and oils unfit for Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah. A story of the Lubliner Rebbe shows the power of a Chanukah light. The Rav then discusses Chanukah as a time of teshuvah and remembrance, the centrality of Hallel, and closes urging everyone to keep his own Chanukah light burning.

en: The Shechinah never descends below ten tefachim, but Chanukah is the exception: its lights must be below ten.
Chanukah was given for Jews who have fallen 'below ten', and its light is kindled in the domain of the sitra achra.
The Chanukah miracle took place at tekufas Teves, the longest night and a time ruled by the sitra achra, and that is when the Shechinah descends to rekindle extinguished souls.
Even souls that Shabbos cannot kindle can be kindled by Chanukah, so every Jew, however distant, can come close to Hashem then.
Chanukah is a time of teshuvah and of remembering the barren, a continuation of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
The essence of Chanukah is Hallel, praising and thanking Hashem, which is why the Rambam brings the laws of Hallel in the laws of Chanukah.
Each Jew is himself a Chanukah light that Hashem kindles, and he must see to it that it is not extinguished.

candidateTopics: Chanukah as a time of teshuvah

title.en: The Shechinah never descends below ten tefachim

summary.en: Speaking three days before Shabbos Chanukah, the Rav brings the Gemara in Sukkah that the Shechinah never came down below ten tefachim, even at Har Sinai. He ties this to the reshus harabim reaching only ten tefachim, to the keruvim, and to the minimum height of a sukkah.

title.en: Chanukah lights below ten, before the Shabbos lights

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah is the exception, lit below ten tefachim, and that it is a weekday Yom Tov, so on Erev Shabbos the Chanukah lights come first. He brings the Tur Bareket that the Chanukah light rises into the Shabbos light, and explains that Chanukah was given for Jews who have fallen below ten.

title.en: Teves, tekufas Teves and Yosef's test

summary.en: The Rav describes how the months were divided between Yaakov and Esav, with Teves and Shevat left to the sitra achra, and explains tekufas Teves, the longest night, as a festival of idolatry going back to Adam HaRishon and the generation of Enosh, and how the calendar shift moved its date. He brings Rashi that Yosef's test came on that day, when he could not use the protection of Torah learning.

title.en: The Shechinah descends to extinguished souls

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Chanukah miracle came in the darkest time, at the end of the month and in the domain of the sitra achra, because the Shechinah then descends below ten to rekindle souls whose Yiddishkeit has gone out. Ner, pesilah and shemen spell neshamah, and oils that may not be lit on Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah.

title.en: The Lubliner Rebbe and the informer

summary.en: The Rav tells how townspeople brought the Lubliner Rebbe a kvitel against an informer; the first night the Rebbe saw his name shining in all worlds and could do nothing, and the next morning the informer died. The Rebbe explained that the man had just lit Chanukah lights, and had he repented, the light would have protected him.

title.en: Chanukah: diamonds, teshuvah and remembrance

summary.en: The Rav says Chanukah is not a time for trips and vacations but, as the Skverer Rebbe said, pure diamonds to be used every minute. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah continues Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and explains Chanukah as a time of remembering the barren, including those barren in Torah and tefillah.

title.en: Hallel is the essence of Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Rambam waits until the laws of Chanukah, at the end of Sefer Zmanim, to bring the laws of Hallel, and answers that Hallel and thanksgiving are the foundation of Chanukah. He explains that every praise of Hashem on Chanukah, including Haneiros Halalu, is part of its Hallel, and laments those who do not put their full strength into it.

title.en: A Shabbos year: keep your own light burning

summary.en: The Rav notes that this year Rosh Hashanah, Shemini Atzeres and both the first and last days of Chanukah fall on Shabbos, and calls on the listeners to use Chanukah and connect to Hashem. Each Jew is himself a Chanukah light; he must not extinguish it after its time, like the ner of Aharon that, the Chidushei HaRim says, still burns. He closes with a brachah.

catalogTitle: קליפת יון - להכחיש בעולם הרוחני - נסיון זמננו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the war of Yavan, foreshadowed by Dinah and Shechem, is a war against emunah fought through tumah and through erasing the name Yisrael, and that this is the test of the generation before Moshiach.

abstract.en: Opening with Vayeshev, the Rav brings the Ramban's principle that the deeds of the Avos are signs for their children, and the Chasam Sofer's reading: having passed through every sign of galus, Yaakov sought a sign of the days of Moshiach, which this world cannot hold, so galus began anew with Yosef. Dinah's abduction stands for the war of Gog uMagog, the war of Yavan. Greek wisdom believes only what the intellect sees, so it fights emunah, which rests on ruach hakodesh and purity; its weapon is tumah, today the trials of arayos and forbidden foods. This explains the pure-oil miracle, and the Rav shows the hidden jar lay where the sotah's dust was taken, the place guarding the purity of Jewish daughters. From Tzidkas HaTzaddik he teaches that a Jew's Jewishness lies in calling himself a Jew; the Greeks, like Shechem and Esav's kiss, sought to erase the name Yisrael. Hence Yaakov forced the angel to concede the name at once, and on Chanukah a Jew should rejoice that he is a Jew.

en: The Rav brings the Ramban's principle that what happened to the Avos is a sign of what will happen to their children, and applies it to Yaakov's life as a map of the whole galus.
The episode of Dinah and Shechem is the sign of the war of Gog uMagog at the end of galus, which is the war of Yavan.
Greek wisdom accepts only what the intellect grasps, and so it wars against emunah; its chief weapon is tumah, which cuts a Jew off from his pure neshamah.
According to Tzidkas HaTzaddik, a Jew's Jewishness rests on his calling himself a Jew, and the Greeks' decree aimed to make Jews deny any portion in the G-d of Israel.
Yaakov refused to wait until Beis El for the angel's concession because the name Yisrael was his weapon for the coming struggle with Shechem, which stands for Yavan.
The Rav says that on Chanukah every Jew should rejoice in having a portion in the G-d of Israel and resolve to strengthen himself in Torah, mitzvos and purity.

title.en: Yaakov's wish for tranquility as a sign

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are signs for their children, traces Yaakov's life through every stage of galus up to the war of Gog uMagog, and gives the Chasam Sofer's explanation of why Yaakov sought tranquility and why galus began again with Yosef.

title.en: Dinah and Yaakov's struggle with the angel

summary.en: The Rav places the trouble of Dinah at the very end of galus, as the war of Gog uMagog, and then turns to Yaakov's struggle with the angel: Yaakov would not release him until he conceded the blessings through the name Yisrael, refusing to wait for Beis El despite the angel's tearful pleas.

title.en: The four kingdoms and the wisdom of Yavan

summary.en: Dinah's trouble is the kingdom of Yavan, one of the four kingdoms of Maoz Tzur. The Rav explains that each galus continues and Hashem gave a weapon against each, and that Greek wisdom, believing only what the intellect sees, fought against emunah.

title.en: Tumah as the weapon against emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that emunah above the intellect comes from ruach hakodesh present in every Jew, so the Greeks attacked it with tumah, which severs a Jew from his pure neshamah. He connects this to 'tamei'im b'yad tehorim' and to the war of Gog uMagog as a war against emunah, citing the Chafetz Chaim on why there would be no more dybbuks.

title.en: The trials of our time: arayos and forbidden foods

summary.en: Weak emunah, the Rav says, stems mainly from two sins that the Torah describes as defiling, arayos and forbidden foods, and these are exactly the trials of today, which earlier generations did not face. A Jew who fights for kedushah in these areas wages the war against Yavan; the Rambam opens the laws of Chanukah with the Greeks bringing tumah upon Jewish daughters.

title.en: The pure oil and where the jar was hidden

summary.en: The Rav asks why a miracle of pure oil was needed if tumah is permitted for the public, and answers that it symbolized the victory of the pure over the impure. He parallels Dinah's defilement with the Greeks defiling all the oils, brings Tosafos that the sealed jar was hidden in the ground, and asks how the Kohen Gadol could bury it under the Heichal's floor, answering from the Mishnah in Sotah about the loose stone from which the sotah's dust was taken.

title.en: Purity of Jewish daughters and the Chazon Ish

summary.en: The jar was guarded in the very place that guards the purity of Jewish daughters, since its purpose was to fight the Greeks' tumah. The Rav tells how the Chazon Ish asked a dentist to wash his hands before treating him, because Torah is acquired only through purity, and concludes that the Greeks attacked emunah through tumah to reach their goal.

title.en: Jewishness rests on calling oneself a Jew

summary.en: The Rav brings Tzidkas HaTzaddik that a Jew's whole Jewishness lies in calling himself a Jew, with the passuk 'uveshem Yisrael yechaneh', the Radvaz on denying one's Jewishness, and an incident from the Toras Chaim about a Jew in Germany asked 'Bist du ein Jude?'.

title.en: Erasing the name Yisrael: Esav's kiss and Shechem

summary.en: The Greeks wanted Jews to deny their portion in the G-d of Israel. The Rav brings the Midrash and the Sfas Emes on Esav, who could not bite Yaakov and so kissed him, as the tactic of today's nations and churches seeking togetherness, and shows the same aim in Shechem's offer to become one people, which the brothers called 'nevalah asah b'Yisrael'.

title.en: The breached soreg and the 25 letters of Shema Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Greeks breached specifically the soreg, and answers that it was the wall separating Jew from gentile and pure from impure. He then explains Chanukah as chaf-heh, the 25 letters of Shema Yisrael: emunah includes believing that one is Yisrael as well as that Hashem is One.

title.en: Why Yaakov insisted on the name Yisrael now

summary.en: Returning to the angel, the Rav explains that both the angel and Yaakov knew Shechem, standing for Yavan, lay ahead; the name Yisrael was the weapon for that war, so the angel wept and Yaakov stood firm. With it Yaakov built the altar 'Kel Elokei Yisrael'. The Rav then says that on Chanukah a Jew should rejoice in being a Jew and accept upon himself strengthening in Torah, mitzvos and purity.

title.en: Chanukah: holiness in the weekday, gifts from Above

summary.en: The Rav describes Chanukah as holiness brought into the weekday and into the darkness of Teves, and as a free gift from Above even to the unworthy. He suggests this is why children receive Chanukah gifts: Hashem gives His children gifts, and the vessels to receive them are a resolution in Torah, mitzvos and joy in being a Jew.

catalogTitle: "ערכתי נר למשיחי" מביאים משיח דוקא ע"י מסירת נפש

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the light of Moshiach hidden in the Chanukah candles is reached only through mesiras nefesh, as Tamar, Yehuda, Yosef and the Chashmonaim showed, and as this generation's trials demand.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the teaching that the Chanukah lights reveal the hidden light, the light of Moshiach: Chanukah is the last mitzvah from the last miracle, and the next miracle is Moshiach, as in 'I have prepared a lamp for My anointed'. The parshiyos of Yehuda and Tamar and of Yosef, read around Chanukah, are the roots of Moshiach ben David and Moshiach ben Yosef. Though the Shechinah never descended below ten tefachim, the Chanukah lamp is placed below ten, like a king who bends down for his fallen son. He then asks why Tamar waited until she was already being taken out to be burned before sending Yehuda the signs. Because she carried Moshiach, and the Satan blocks Moshiach with all his strength, as he did with Er and Onan; the only counter is mesiras nefesh, here the shame Yehuda accepted. Yosef too had to pass a test of mesiras nefesh. The Chashmonaim earned the Chanukah light the same way, and in today's ikvesa d'meshicha, with unprecedented trials, every bit of mesiras nefesh brings Moshiach closer.

en: The Chanukah lights hold the hidden light of Moshiach; Chanukah is the last mitzvah from the last miracle, and the next miracle is the coming of Moshiach.
The Chanukah lamp is placed below ten tefachim, where the Shechinah otherwise never descends, because Hashem lowers Himself to His children in galus as a king bends down for his son.
Tamar knew she carried the root of Moshiach and understood that the Satan blocks Moshiach, so the only way was mesiras nefesh: Yehuda's public shame and her own readiness to be burned.
Yosef too had to pass a test of mesiras nefesh and accept disgrace before he could bring Moshiach ben Yosef into the world.
The Chashmonaim earned the Chanukah light through mesiras nefesh, and in today's ikvesa d'meshicha nothing can be achieved without it; every small act of mesiras nefesh adds to Moshiach's coming.
