title.en: The light of Moshiach in the Chanukah candles

summary.en: The Rav brings that lighting the Chanukah candles reveals the hidden light of Moshiach, and that Chanukah, the last mitzvah from the last miracle, points to the next miracle, Moshiach. He connects the parshiyos of Yehuda and Tamar and of Yosef, read at this time, to Moshiach ben David and Moshiach ben Yosef.

title.en: Below ten tefachim: Hashem descends to His children

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the rule that the Shechinah never descended below ten tefachim with the mitzvah to place the Chanukah lamp below ten, and explains it with a parable of a king who bends down only for his own son. Chanukah, a weekday yom tov of galus, is Hashem visiting His people with a taste of Moshiach; and both Yehuda and Yosef first went down, the descent before the rise.

title.en: Why Tamar waited until the last moment

summary.en: The Rav asks why Tamar, already taken out to be burned, waited until then to send Yehuda his seal, cord and staff, putting him to a terrible test before the beis din of Yitzchak, Yaakov and Shem. He describes the greatness of Yehuda's admission, which Yaakov praised, and begins the answer: Tamar knew she carried Moshiach, and the Satan is Moshiach's greatest obstacle.

title.en: The Satan targets the bearer of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav asks how Er, Yehuda's firstborn and Yaakov's grandson, fell into so grave a sin, and answers that Moshiach was to come from him, so the Satan concentrated on him. He supports this with the Tosafos Yom Tov on the miracle of the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur and Tosafos on the shofar confusing the Satan, brings Rabbeinu Bechaye that Er and Onan returned as Peretz and Zerach, and concludes that only mesiras nefesh takes away the Satan's power.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh through shame: Tamar, Yehuda and Yosef

summary.en: The Rav quotes the Imrei Emes and the Belzer Rav that in the time before Moshiach nothing is attained without mesiras nefesh. Tamar understood that Yehuda had to accept public shame, which Chazal liken to bloodshed, and she was ready to be burned rather than shame him; so Peretz was born and the Satan could not interfere. Yosef likewise had to pass a test of mesiras nefesh and disgrace before bringing Ephraim into the world.

title.en: Chanukah, our generation and its trials

summary.en: The Rav explains that unlike the other rabbinic mitzvos, which were a gift, the Chanukah light was earned by the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh. In ikvesa d'meshicha, which the Chofetz Chaim said had begun, every bit of mesiras nefesh, even giving up one's will, adds to Moshiach's coming, and the Satan answers with trials no generation has had, the culture of the street, television and the internet.

title.en: Where to flee today, and Zos Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav calls going out to the street a war like the Chashmonaim's, brings the Satmar Rav's question on the Rambam about leaving a bad place and the answer that the yeshiva is the refuge, and speaks of choosing friends and a livelihood. Customs alone will not carry a Jew through, he says; the Chanukah lamp faces the mezuzah with Shema's mesiras nefesh. He closes asking for resolutions on Zos Chanukah, refusing the yetzer hara as Yosef did, and with a brachah for Moshiach.

catalogTitle: A Deeper Understanding of נחלת בני ראובן ובני גד and the Hidden Kedushah of the Three Weeks

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Bnei Reuven and Bnei Gad sensed that the land east of the Jordan holds the hidden, higher kedushah of the Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni, which corresponds to the Three Weeks, whose concealed holiness will be revealed when Mashiach comes.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Moshe Rabbeinu's rebuke of Bnei Gad and Bnei Reuven and asks why he says 'I know you have much livestock' and why the Torah stresses 'atzum me'od'. Following the Midrash and Sfas Emes, their portion was truly theirs, but they hurried to take it. He then builds a structure: of the ten maamaros the first three are beyond grasp, and of the ten nations promised to Avraham the Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni (Ammon, Moav, Esav) are hidden under a great tumah that covers a greater kedushah. These correspond to the Three Weeks before the seven weeks of consolation. Reuven the firstborn and Gad, the tribe of Eliyahu, are bound to this 'reishis', the land of the future. Their sheep were lofty souls, which Moshe knew. The Rav closes that the Three Weeks are days of digging for hidden kedushah through Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

en: According to the Sfas Emes, the land east of the Jordan was truly the portion of Bnei Reuven and Bnei Gad; their fault was only that they hurried to take it instead of waiting for it to be given al pi haTorah.

A person's nefesh extends into his belongings, and Hashem's hashgachah gives each person exactly what is his; one who grabs his portion dishonestly would have received it anyway, and loses it because he hurried.

Of the ten maamaros the first three are beyond human grasp, and likewise of the ten nations promised to Avraham the Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni are not yet accessible; they will become Klal Yisrael's when Mashiach comes.

The ten weeks before Rosh Hashanah parallel the ten nations: the Three Weeks correspond to the hidden Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni, and the seven weeks of consolation to the seven nations already conquered.
Reuven, the firstborn, is 'reishis', and Gad is the tribe of Eliyahu and the geulah; both are bound to the days of Mashiach, which is why they wanted this land.
The Rav explains that their great livestock were lofty souls of the future, and Moshe Rabbeinu's 'I know' means that he knew their secret, though they should not have put it into words.
The Three Weeks are days of digging: through extra effort in Torah, tefillah and tzedakah one can uncover the kedushah hidden beneath their darkness.

candidateTopics: Eliyahu and the tribe of Gad

title.en: Why 'I know' and why 'atzum me'od'

summary.en: The Rav presents Moshe Rabbeinu's rebuke that Bnei Gad and Bnei Reuven put their sheep before their children, and asks why Moshe says 'I know you have much livestock' and why the Torah stresses 'atzum me'od'. He brings the Midrash that they hurried for their portion and were the first exiled, and the Sfas Emes that the portion was truly theirs but should have come al pi haTorah.

title.en: What is yours will come to you

summary.en: The Rav explains that a person's nefesh extends into his belongings, and that Hashem divides everything with exactness so each gets what is his, illustrated with a cup of soda. One who uses dishonest means for something would have gotten it anyway, and because he hurried he loses it; so too Bnei Reuven and Bnei Gad.

title.en: The ten maamaros and the hidden first three

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah that the world was created with ten maamaros and the Gemara that 'Bereishis' is also a maamar, showing how lofty it is. The first three are beyond our grasp and are heavenly, while the last seven are earthly and familiar to us.

title.en: Keini, Kenizi, Kadmoni: kedushah under tumah

summary.en: The Rav explains that of the ten nations promised to Avraham, the Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni (Ammon, Moav and Esav) are mentioned only once and will be Klal Yisrael's only in the days of Mashiach. They are covered by a great tumah like an orlah, and following the Sfas Emes and the Chesed L'Avraham their hidden kedushah is greater than that of Eretz Yisrael proper; the land of Reuven and Gad was a piece of Ammon and Moav taken through Sichon.

title.en: The Three Weeks as the hidden three lands

summary.en: The Rav maps the ten weeks before Rosh Hashanah onto the ten nations: the seven weeks of consolation are graspable, while the Three Weeks are the Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni and will be the most joyful days when Mashiach comes. He brings the Avodas Yisrael on 'kol rodfeha hisiguha bein hametzarim', says learning and davening are harder now but reach higher, and gives a mashal of embroidery on a black cloth.

title.en: Reuven the firstborn and Gad of Eliyahu

summary.en: The Rav says the hidden world of the first three is the source of good concealed in suffering, pointing to the Igeres HaKodesh. He then explains that Reuven, as bechor, is 'reishis' but lost the bechorah through haste; in the time of tikun every blemish will be washed out and he will regain it. Gad too is bound to Mashiach, since Eliyahu comes from Gad.

title.en: Gad saw 'reishis'; half of Menashe

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk in Vezos Habrachah that Gad 'saw reishis' because Moshe is buried there, and adds that they wanted Moshe's conquest rather than Yehoshua's. Gimmel-Reish of the first three stands for Gad and Reuven, and the half tribe of Menashe, who also lost a bechorah, joins them; Esav, the third, remains untouchable until Mashiach.

title.en: Rashi's 'koach maasav' and the Kadmoni

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi's question why the Torah begins with Bereishis and the answer 'koach maasav higid l'amo', and the passuk that the saviors will judge Har Esav. He explains that Esav is the klipah over the kedushah of Bereishis, so the Torah's opening hints that Klal Yisrael will one day receive the Kadmoni and the whole world; the answer to the nations is that their complaint over the seven nations misses the point.

title.en: The forty days of the spies and Tammuz

summary.en: The Rav brings Rav Shimshon of Ostropoli on 'vehayamim yemei bikurei anavim': the letters before 'anavim' spell the name of the Samech Mem, so these forty days, Tammuz and the nine days, are in his domain. He supports that the nine days belong to Tammuz from the Chasam Sofer and the Bnei Yissaschar, and adds gematrios linking these days to Har Esav and the Kadmoni.

title.en: Souls of the days of Mashiach

summary.en: The Rav says such lofty matters must be learned by way of drush, and proposes that Bnei Reuven and Bnei Gad were souls of the days of Mashiach, so their instincts told them, as the Sfas Emes says, that this land was theirs. He compares it to belief in techiyas hameisim being a sign of having a share in it, and explains Moshe's 'I know' as 'I know your secret'.

title.en: Yaakov's sheep and the Yismach Moshe

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal that Yaakov's sheep were holy souls he drew out of Lavan's domain, and tells how the Yismach Moshe remembered his earlier gilgulim, including the dispute of Korach and being a sheep of Yaakov Avinu. From this and the Midrash on Yaakov's 600,000 flocks he concludes that the livestock of these tribes were lofty souls of the future.

title.en: Hidden light: 'I found David in Sedom'

summary.en: The Rav explains Moshe's words: he knew how great their sheep were, but they should not have said it openly. He then says hidden good lies in the Three Weeks: Mashiach is born on Tisha B'Av, Shiva Asar B'Tammuz is destined to be a 'chag', and the Midrash finds David in Sedom, with great souls hidden under refuse. He calls these forty days of digging for kedushah.

title.en: Yovel at the end of Bamidbar and the avodah

summary.en: The Rav notes that the word yovel, meaning return to the root, appears twenty-one times in the Torah, the last at the end of Bamidbar, and follows the tzaddikim's custom of finding a hint that Mashiach comes this year. He closes that Tammuz and Rosh Chodesh Menachem Av hint to Melech HaMashiach and calls for hard work in Torah, tefillah and tzedakah in these weeks.

catalogTitle: כשמדליקין הנרות נעשה ככהן וביתו כביהמ"ק

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that when a Jew lights the Chanukah candles his home becomes a Beis Hamikdash and he himself becomes like a kohen, and that the light of Chanukah, the hidden light of the days of Moshiach, comes down into the darkness of exile and brings blessing in Torah and the habit of thanking Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the passuk 'Ashrei kol yerei Hashem' as Rav Hirsch reads it: the warmth of the Jewish home, which needs nothing from outside, and the shul and beis medrash, from which Torah's warmth is brought home. On Chanukah, he says, 'Yevarechecha Hashem mi-Tziyon' comes true even on a weekday: lighting the candles is a remembrance of the Mikdash, so the home becomes a Beis Hamikdash and every Jew becomes a kohen. He ties this to the hidden light of Moshiach's days, to the Rambam's ruling that lighting the menorah needs no kohen, and to the name Chashmonaim. He explains Chanukah as a family mitzvah like the Shabbos candles, and why one may not benefit from its light: it comes down into the weekday darkness of exile. He closes with Chanukah as a time of blessing for the barren in body and in Torah, chiddushim that give rise to chiddushim, and hallel and thanks.

en: Lighting the Chanukah candles is a remembrance of the Mikdash, so for the half hour they burn every Jew's home becomes a Beis Hamikdash.
Since he performs a service of the Mikdash, every Jew who lights becomes like a kohen, a foretaste of the days of Moshiach when all Jews will be kohanim.
Ner Chanukah is a mitzvah on the family, like ner Shabbos, and through both a Jew can see 'the good of Yerushalayim' in his own home even in exile.
The Chanukah light is the hidden light kept for the future; on Shabbos a Jew rises to a higher world, while on Chanukah that higher world comes down into weekday exile.
Chanukah is a time of blessing for those 'barren' in body or spirit: for tefillos that went unanswered and for Torah learning that bore no chiddushim.
The heart of Chanukah is hallel and hoda'ah, and the Rav says one must accustom oneself to thank Hashem for every small thing.

candidateTopics: the home as a Beis Hamikdash

title.en: The warmth of the Jewish home

summary.en: Following Rav Hirsch on 'Ashrei kol yerei Hashem', the Rav contrasts the content, warm Jewish home with the gentile search for excitement outside, and adds the shul and beis medrash as the community's home from which the fire of Torah is brought back. Every passuk, he says, speaks anew to every generation and every soul.

title.en: The home becomes a Beis Hamikdash

summary.en: The Rav notes that the main miracle of the day was the victory in the war, and explains that lighting Chanukah candles is a remembrance of the menorah in the Mikdash, so that for the half hour they burn each home becomes a Beis Hamikdash. Yerushalayim visits every Jew on Shabbos; the chiddush of Chanukah is that it comes on a weekday.

title.en: Matisyahu, and every Jew a kohen

summary.en: Using the triad of time, place and soul, the Rav calls Matisyahu the soul of Chanukah and notes that his name equals 'Beis Hamikdash' in gematria. Whoever lights does a Mikdash service and becomes a kohen, a glimpse of the hidden light of Moshiach's days when all Jews will be kohanim; he explains through this the Rambam's ruling that lighting the menorah needs no kohen.

title.en: The name Chashmonaim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer that Chashmon hints at oil for eight days, then offers his own reading: as Haman resented the Jewish festivals and Purim was added, so the Greeks tried to abolish chodesh, Shabbos and milah and the mitzvah of ner Chanukah was added, all four hinted in the letters of Chashmon. He adds that the name also hints at 'kohen' for eight days.

title.en: A mitzvah of the family

summary.en: The Rav explains that ner Chanukah, 'ner ish u-veiso', is a mitzvah on the household, not on the individual like tefillin, and so it fits the passuk about the Jewish family. Ner Shabbos is also a family obligation and Shabbos is itself a Mikdash; the chiddush of Chanukah is that this comes on a weekday.

title.en: Why one may not use the Chanukah light

summary.en: The Rav asks why one may not benefit from the Chanukah light, the hidden light kept for the tzaddikim, when the Shabbos light is also hidden light and one may enjoy it, learning by it with a special Shabbos sweetness. He answers that on Shabbos a Jew is raised to a higher world, while on Chanukah the higher world comes down into exile, in the darkest time of the year.

title.en: Lighting inside as the street invades

summary.en: The Rav explains that the candles were once lit facing the public domain, but as Moshiach's time nears the public domain pushes into the Jewish home, today through television, radio and the internet, so one must at least light up the home. Even in such darkness, through ner Shabbos and ner Chanukah a Jew can see 'the good of Yerushalayim' at home.

title.en: Remembering the barren, and blessing as increase

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah, like Rosh Hashanah, is a time when the barren are remembered, in body and in spirit: unanswered tefillos and Torah without blessing. With the Maharal he explains that bracha means increase, and he cites the Bnei Yissaschar that one who says chiddushei Torah fulfils the mitzvah of having children.

title.en: Chiddushim from chiddushim; hallel and thanks

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on why David called Achitofel his rebbe for two things: a chiddush from kedushah gives rise to further chiddushim, and that is 'banim l'vanecha'. He then says the root of Chanukah is hallel and hoda'ah, as in the days of Moshiach only the korban todah will remain, and one must accustom oneself to thank Hashem for every small thing; he shows this from the Rambam's placement of the laws of hallel in hilchos Chanukah.

catalogTitle: א) יו"ט למעלה מן הגבולות של עוה"ז

oneLiner.en: The Rav notes that the Rambam calls the mitzvah of Chanukah a cherished mitzvah, and later speaks of Chanukah as a time of adding, of going further into kedushah.

abstract.en: Only fragments of this shiur survive in the transcript. The Rav opens with the Rambam's statement that the mitzvah of Chanukah is a mitzvah chaviva, a very cherished mitzvah, and points out that the Rambam does not use this expression about other mitzvos; by Chanukah, he says, something is found that is not found elsewhere. Most of what follows is lost. In a garbled middle stretch he speaks of engaging in holy matters for the sake of Hashem and mentions a count reaching thirty-six. Toward the end he describes Chanukah as the time of mosif v'holech, of adding each night, and speaks of adding in kedushah and entering further into it.

en: The Rav cites the Rambam that the mitzvah of Chanukah is a mitzvah chaviva, a very cherished mitzvah.
He points out that the Rambam does not use this expression about the other mitzvos.
The Rav describes Chanukah as the time of mosif v'holech, of adding from night to night.
He speaks of adding in kedushah and entering further into kedushah.
